assessments.operationalization: Build phylogenies containing cave and nearby surface taxa from North America and Europe, and compare whether cave species cluster by continent or cave habitat. Repeated sister relationships to same-continent surface lineages support the prediction; a transcontinental cave clade would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank

candidate_datasets.role: continental and cave occurrence records

obstacles: Some cave taxa lack sequence data or reliable locality metadata.

assessments.rationale: The prediction is a direct phylogeographic comparison and abundant public sequence and occurrence records exist. Standard phylogenetic analyses can resolve it across many independent cave clades within weeks.

assessments.operationalization: Partition explained variation in range limits between climate and biotic-interaction predictors across many species, supplemented by transplants or invasions beyond native boundaries. A median biotic contribution at least as large as climate supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: species distributions and co-occurrence patterns

assessments.operationalization: Estimate within-individual and genetic covariance in size, shape or developmental perturbation among homologous bilateral or serial parts. candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank

obstacles: Failure to detect utility does not establish that a character is useless.

assessments.operationalization: Identify repeated transitions in which an organ became functionally superfluous and reconstruct its size, energetic cost and correlated changes in other parts. candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: morphological character matrices spanning organ-loss transitions

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic framework for repeated transitions

assessments.operationalization: Across species, estimate within-species variance in part number and regress it on mean repeat number, comparing serial structures with low-copy homologues. A robust positive relationship and near constancy at low copy number support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: coded counts of serial structures across taxa

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: specimens for vertebral and other repeated-part counts

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad

assessments.operationalization: Quantify how exceptional a species' trait is relative to congeners and relate that value to within-species trait variance, distinguishing species-specific from clade-wide novelty. A positive phylogenetically controlled association supports the rule.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: comparative morphological characters among allied species

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: specimen-level anatomy for trait and variance estimates

assessments.operationalization: For traits used in taxonomy, compare within-species variation of species-diagnostic characters with genus-shared characters after scaling and measurement-error correction. candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic morphological character matrices

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: multiple specimens for quantitative character variation

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank

assessments.operationalization: Within genera or families, compare standardized among-species divergence and within-species variance for secondary sexual traits versus other morphology. Larger values for sexual traits support the claim; comparable or smaller divergence refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Macaulay Library
candidate_datasets.role: sex-labelled images and sounds for avian ornaments and displays

candidate_datasets.role: specimen-level sexually dimorphic morphology

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank

candidate_datasets.role: fossil Equus occurrences and taxonomy

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database

assessments.operationalization: Estimate range widths and overlap-zone widths for geographically replacing close relatives, and fit abundance changes toward each boundary. candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: regional late Tertiary fossil occurrences

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF

assessments.rationale: Every component has measurable consequences and substantial public data, but the full causal synthesis cannot be cleanly identified from one integrated record. Existing analyses can resolve subsets and compare restricted process models.

assessments.operationalization: Fit trait and interaction models for coadapted structures (foraging morphology, host and pollinator links) against climate- and diet-only models. The external-conditions account would be supported if climate and food variables left little residual association between the coadapted traits and the partner organisms; it would be weakened if biotic partners explained that structure after climate and phylogeny were controlled.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: plant functional traits for comparing climate-only models with traits tied to other organisms

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: climate layers as the external-conditions predictors

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: recorded host, pollinator, and consumer links for coadaptation case studies

obstacles: What counts as a complex coadaptation, and as fully accounting for it, has to be stipulated before any model comparison is decisive.
Phylogenetic inertia and historical biogeography produce trait-environment correlations that mimic a direct climatic explanation.
Quantitative functional morphology for animals such as woodpeckers is scattered, so most tests would use a biased subset of well-studied interactions.
assessments.rationale: Climate layers, trait compilations, and interaction records exist and can support a residual test for some well-known plant-animal systems. They do not cover the full range of coadapted structures, and several plausible mappings from Darwin's wording onto variables compete. Even a large residual for biotic partners would leave room for correlated selection and unmeasured food variables, so the result would be informative mainly for particular systems.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate low-density population growth and the surplus of births over replacement from matrix models and fecundity schedules, then ask whether small heritable advantages predict higher survival or reproductive success in the same populations. Persistent geometric potential with realized populations held far below it would support the overproduction premise; a general failure of slight heritable differences to predict fitness would challenge the selection step only if 'profitable' is defined independently of the fitness outcome.

candidate_datasets.name: COMPADRE and COMADRE
candidate_datasets.role: stage-structured fecundity and survival for potential versus realized increase

candidate_datasets.name: Living Planet Index
candidate_datasets.role: multi-year abundance trajectories showing populations are not at unbounded geometric increase

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fecundity and life-history fields for a large animal clade

obstacles: A variation that is profitable to its bearer is already defined by improved survival or reproduction, so that half of the statement is nearly analytic.
Public demographic databases rarely pair individual-level heritable differences with fitness in the same rows.
Density dependence, measurement of 'slight' variation, and publication bias in selection studies all change the apparent strength of the result.
assessments.rationale: Open life-history compilations can test overproduction for hundreds of plants and animals, which is only part of the syllogism. The step from a profitable slight variation to a better chance of survival is difficult to refute without an independent definition of profit, and heritability-plus-fitness tables are not in one downloadable archive. A small team could test the demographic premise quickly and would still be short of a non-circular test of the whole mechanism.

assessments.operationalization: Measure genus- and species-level extinction rates and morphological disparity through time in the fossil record, and sister-lineage trait divergence on time-calibrated trees. The pattern side would be supported if less persistent forms disappear while disparity among survivors grows; attributing both patterns to natural selection would require a fitness proxy that outpredicts abiotic drivers.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences for extinction and morphological disparity through time

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: extant phylogenies for lineage divergence of form

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: divergence times to place splitting against geological intervals

obstacles: 'Less improved' has no direct fossil measurement and is easily confused with rarity or short stratigraphic range.
Mass extinctions, climate, and sampling intensity produce extinction and apparent divergence without a selection mechanism.
Preservation bias truncates last occurrences and inflates late Cenozoic diversity.
assessments.rationale: Extinction tallies and disparity curves are standard products of open fossil and tree databases, so the pattern half can be examined for well-skeletonized groups. Linking those patterns specifically to selection, rather than to environmental forcing or sampling, needs a fitness measure the occurrence tables do not contain. The analysis is feasible for marine animals and much weaker for the full scope of organic beings.

assessments.operationalization: Test whether species placed in the same genus form clades on sequence data, using concordance across independent loci rather than a single assumed tree, and whether the inferred ancestral node is older than the living members and matched by extinct fossil relatives. Independent creation or immutability would be favoured if genetic similarity were not hierarchically nested or if living species were routinely ancestral to their congeners; shared ancestry from earlier, now extinct lineages would favour the historical claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: synthetic genus-level phylogenies and taxonomy for monophyly tests

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: homologous sequences for gene-tree concordance independent of one classification

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: extinct congeners and stratigraphic ages for the 'generally extinct' ancestor

obstacles: Genus limits are themselves revised using phylogenies, so a test must freeze a pre-molecular classification or use rank-free clades.
Many named genera still lack sequence data, and the fossil record is sparse for soft-bodied groups and plants.
Hybrid speciation and incomplete lineage sorting produce local non-monophyly without restoring independent creation.
assessments.rationale: Public sequences, a synthetic tree, and fossil occurrences already contain the variables needed to test shared ancestry and extinct stems for a large fraction of named plant and animal genera. Concordance across loci and fossils keeps the test from simply assuming the tree that classification built. Coverage is incomplete, especially outside vertebrates and vascular plants, but it is broad enough that a standard comparative analysis could confirm or refute the generalization rather than only a narrow proxy.

assessments.operationalization: Partition evolutionary change in form among selection, drift, and other inheritance systems, using quantitative-genetic and comparative estimates, and treat sequence substitution rates only as a modern side test. Selection would count as the main cause if it explained more of the phenotypic change than drift, mutation bias, and plasticity combined, while still leaving a non-zero residue for other causes; a predominance of neutral or plastic change would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: coding sequences for selection-versus-drift ratios, a molecular proxy rather than a direct phenotypic partition

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: annotated genomes and variant consequences for a handful of model and domestic species

obstacles: 'Main cause of modification' needs an agreed currency that sums across traits, species, and timescales.
Darwin's modification is change of organisms, so a molecular neutrality test answers a reinterpreted question.
Estimates of selection on phenotypes are scattered through papers and cover a tiny slice of traits.
assessments.rationale: Sequence archives make a neutrality-versus-selection contrast routine for genes, and that contrast can show that selection is not the sole process. They do not measure the share of organismal modification caused by selection across living things. Several defensible partitions give different answers, and assembling a phenotypic sample would take months of harmonization for a still-narrow subset.

assessments.operationalization: Compare within-variety coefficients of variation, or genomic heterozygosity, for homologous characters in long-cultivated populations and in wild populations of the parent species. Greater within-group dispersion in the domestic samples would support the contrast; equal or smaller domestic dispersion across a pre-registered trait set would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: European Variation Archive
candidate_datasets.role: within-population genetic variation for domestic species and some wild relatives

candidate_datasets.name: Domestic Animal Diversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: breed inventories used to define the domestic varieties being compared

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: reference variation for major crops and livestock with sequenced wild relatives

obstacles: Modern breed standards have deliberately reduced within-breed differences since the nineteenth century.
Genetic heterozygosity and visible individual differences can move in opposite directions after a domestication bottleneck.
Individual-level phenotypic measurements are scattered, while public sequence archives over-represent a few commercial species.
assessments.rationale: The comparison itself maps cleanly onto within-group dispersion, and public variant archives plus breed lists cover the main livestock and crop species. A full phenotypic test of older cultivated varieties against wild relatives still has to be compiled from studies and gene banks. The contrast can discriminate the stated pattern from its opposite for that subset, with the caveat that today's uniform breeds are a biased sample of what Darwin observed.

assessments.operationalization: Hold ancestry constant and compare phenotypic or mutational variance of lines reared in uniform ancestral environments versus novel, less uniform ones, alongside a selection-relaxed control. A causal role for conditions would be supported if environmental novelty raised heritable variance when selection and hybridization were matched; no increase, or an increase explained by relaxed selection alone, would count against the stated cause.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: trait values for wild and cultivated plants, a descriptive proxy rather than a controlled conditions contrast

obstacles: Relaxed selection, hybridization, and larger census sizes are confounded with the change in conditions under domestication.
Public trait databases mostly store species means, not variances from common-garden designs.
The relevant experiments exist as scattered supplements and cover few domesticated species.
assessments.rationale: The causal contrast is definable, but the datasets that are easy to download record where cultivated plants differ, not whether uneven conditions produced that variability. A honest test needs common-garden or mutation-accumulation designs that are not assembled in one open archive. Existing compilations can describe domestic versus wild dispersion and leave the mechanism entangled with selection and crossing.

assessments.operationalization: Measure the share of new heritable variation attributable to pre-conception environmental effects on gametes, relative to spontaneous mutation and recombination, across domesticated and confined species, and compare environmental sensitivity of reproductive failure with sensitivity of other organ systems. The reproductive-element account would be supported if that pathway explained more new variation than the alternatives and if reproduction failed under milder environmental change than other systems.
obstacles: No open database records pre-conception environments, gamete state, and offspring heritable variance for the same individuals.
Zoo and studbook reproductive-failure records that might speak to sensitivity of the reproductive system are not generally public.
Epigenetic and mutation-rate studies cover a few model species and are not harmonized.
assessments.rationale: The mechanism can be stated in modern variables, as environmentally induced germline change versus ordinary mutation. Public archives do not contain the paired measurements that would show it is the most frequent cause, or that the reproductive system is uniquely sensitive, across animals and plants under domestication. A test would require new compilation at best and new designs for most species.

assessments.operationalization: Compare wing-bone and leg-bone proportions, scaled to the whole skeleton, between domestic ducks and wild mallards, and extend the same use-matched contrast to other domestic species with known activity differences. A skeletal shift in the predicted direction would support the phenotypic example; inheritance of an acquired effect of use would require offspring of exercised and unexercised parents to differ when the offspring themselves share the same activity.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D skeletal media from which limb-bone proportions could be measured when domestic and wild ducks are present

candidate_datasets.name: VertNet
candidate_datasets.role: museum specimen records locating wild and domestic duck skeletons

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: aggregated specimen metadata for a broader domestic-versus-wild osteological sample

obstacles: Specimen databases record that a skeleton exists more often than they record bone weights.
A domestic-wild difference is equally expected under selection on standing variation and under phenotypic plasticity.
A design that isolates inheritance of acquired use from selection is essentially absent from open archives.
assessments.rationale: Museum and scan portals make the duck bone comparison a restricted, partly compilable test, and the same portals thin out quickly for other domestic animals. They do not separate use-inheritance from selection or from rearing conditions, which is the mechanistic content. Discriminating that mechanism would take breeding designs that are not sitting in a public dataset.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate genetic correlations, or correlated responses, between a selected target trait and traits that were not selection criteria, across breeding populations and crop evaluation trials. Widespread non-zero correlated change would support the expectation; a regular pattern of target traits changing alone would refute the 'almost certainly' clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals
candidate_datasets.role: pleiotropic Mendelian phenotypes in domestic species, a large-effect subset of correlated modification

candidate_datasets.name: European Variation Archive
candidate_datasets.role: variants linked to selected traits where multi-trait effects are annotated

candidate_datasets.name: USDA GRIN
candidate_datasets.role: multi-descriptor crop evaluations that can show which organs differ among selected accessions

obstacles: Genetic-correlation matrices are published study by study rather than in one livestock-and-crop archive.
Mendelian pleiotropy over-represents genes of large effect relative to the slight variations Darwin emphasized.
Unintentional change can also come from drift and linkage, which mimic correlation of growth.
assessments.rationale: Correlated response is a standard variable, and pleiotropy catalogues plus multi-trait crop descriptors already show that selected changes often travel with other characters in major domestic species. Those sources are a subset of domesticated animals and plants, and turning them into a fair test of 'almost certainly' means months of harmonizing breeding studies. The null of independent modification is discriminable where multi-trait data exist.

assessments.operationalization: Regress offspring age at first expression of a peculiarity on parental age at first expression, allowing an earlier-offspring class, for inherited diseases and life-stage traits. A positive age match, with a minority of earlier offspring onsets, would support the rule; ages of onset scattered independently of the parent's age would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals
candidate_datasets.role: inherited animal phenotypes, some with age-of-onset notes, mostly unpaired across generations

obstacles: Many characters can be expressed at only one developmental stage, so a matching age is obligatory.
OMIA rarely pairs a specific parent's onset age with the offspring's onset age.
Shared rearing environment can align ages of onset without an inheritance rule about timing.
assessments.rationale: Age-of-onset correlation is a clear statistic, and an animal Mendelian catalogue contains pieces of it for domestic species. It is not a parent-offspring age table, and plants are barely represented, so coverage is a thin subset of the stated scope. Developmental necessity and shared environment keep a positive correlation from uniquely supporting a special inheritance-timing rule.

assessments.operationalization: Place domestic breeds and closely allied wild congeners in one morphospace and one genetic-distance matrix, then compare the axes that separate breeds with the axes that separate species and compare the magnitudes. Similar axes with smaller breed distances would support the statement; breed differences concentrated on different axes, or as large as species differences, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D morphology for a subset of domestic breeds and wild relatives

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: genomic distances among breeds and wild congeners for sequenced species

candidate_datasets.name: Domestic Animal Diversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: breed lists and coarse descriptors defining the domestic races

obstacles: 'Same manner' depends on which characters are measured and on how morphospaces are aligned.
Breed descriptors are categorical and uneven, while 3D coverage is sparse.
Fertility when crossed and monstrous development, which the statement sets aside, are not in the same tables as shape.
assessments.rationale: Genomic distances and scattered 3D scans can compare some breed pairs with some congeneric species, which is a proxy for 'same manner' and 'lesser degree'. No open dataset systematically measures the same characters in domestic races and wild congeners across animals and plants. The qualitative wording admits several morphometric operationalizations, so a single result would be only partly decisive.

assessments.operationalization: Domesticate a matched set of previously wild species, equal in number, taxonomic spread, and generations to existing domesticated productions, and compare their accumulated phenotypic variance. Equal average variance would support the prediction; systematically less variance in the new domesticates, after matching generations and diversity of conditions, would refute it.
obstacles: No public experiment has kept a taxonomically matched set of wild species under domestication for a number of generations comparable to ancient crops and livestock.
Recent domestications such as farmed fish differ in breeding intensity and are documented case by case.
Variance under domestication confounds generations of breeding with intentional selection intensity.
assessments.rationale: The prediction is clear enough to score once generation depth and taxonomic spread are matched. That matched series does not exist in any open database, and a few recent domestication genome projects are not a substitute for it. Resolving the counterfactual would require new long-running breeding records rather than a reanalysis of current archives.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate ancestry graphs for worldwide dog breeds against wild canids using public genomes. Descent from several wild species would be supported by substantial founding ancestry from two or more canid species; a single founding species, with only later minor admixture, would refute that reading.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: assembled canid genomes and reference sequences for dogs, wolves, and other wild species

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: raw reads for breeds and wild canids, including ancient samples, for admixture analyses

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: dog genome annotation and comparative alignments used to call ancestry-informative variants

obstacles: Extinct Pleistocene wolf populations are unevenly sampled, so an unsampled source can look like a missing species.
Darwin's geographical 'species' may correspond to wolf populations that current taxonomy treats as one species.
Modern breed admixture with coyotes or jackals can be mistaken for a separate domestication origin.
assessments.rationale: Dog and wild canid genomes are public in the sequence archives, and ancestry graphs are a standard analysis a small team can rerun. The data cover major breed groups and the living wild species Darwin would have considered, with real gaps for extinct wolves. Those gaps and the species-versus-population ambiguity lower discriminating power without changing the fact that a single-species versus multi-species origin is directly testable now.

assessments.operationalization: Place domestic pigeon breeds and wild Columba species, including geographical forms of Columba livia, on a multilocus tree and an admixture graph. Nesting of all breed groups inside C. livia would support single origin from the rock-pigeon; breed groups scattered among other wild Columba species would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: pigeon and other Columba genome assemblies for phylogenetic placement of breeds

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: resequencing reads across fancy breeds and wild rock-pigeons

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: annotated rock-pigeon genome used as the reference for breed variants

obstacles: Not every fancy breed and not every geographical subspecies of C. livia is sequenced.
Feral pigeons and later hybridization can obscure an originally mixed origin.
A few breeds differ by large-effect mutations, which does not by itself imply a different wild species.
assessments.rationale: The named ancestor and the alternative of several wild stocks are both directly readable from public pigeon and Columba sequences. Major breed groups and the rock-pigeon have already been deposited, so a reanalysis is weeks of standard phylogenomics rather than a new collecting program. Incomplete sampling of obscure breeds and wild subspecies limits certainty at the margin and does not block a confirm-or-refute test of the stated origin.

assessments.operationalization: Classify breed-defining differences by genetic architecture and by the time series of allele frequencies from ancient to modern animals: many successive small shifts versus a single large-effect origin. A predominance of multi-locus, temporally accumulated change aligned with breeding goals would support accumulative selection; a predominance of one-step sports that already match the finished breed would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: ancient and modern domestic genomes for allele-frequency trajectories

candidate_datasets.name: European Variation Archive
candidate_datasets.role: present-day variant catalogues for polygenic versus large-effect breed differences

candidate_datasets.name: Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals
candidate_datasets.role: catalogued large-effect breed mutations that represent the sudden-origin alternative

obstacles: Ancient DNA time series exist for a few species and preserve only part of the phenotype.
Both large-effect mutations and polygenic selection are real, so 'the key cause' is a balance, not a yes-or-no.
Archaeological morphology cannot show that a breeder, rather than natural selection or drift, accumulated the changes.
assessments.rationale: Public genomes and a Mendelian catalogue can show, for major domestic species, whether breed differences look accumulated or single-step. That is a proxy for the historical mechanism, and it covers a minority of domesticated animals and plants. Mixed architectures mean the result can reject a purely sudden origin more readily than it can crown accumulative selection as the key cause.

assessments.operationalization: For cultivated species, partition among-variety trait variance into the organ that breeders selected (leaf, flower, or fruit) and organs that were not the target. A larger share of variance in the selected organ would support the rule; similar variance in selected and unselected organs would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: USDA GRIN
candidate_datasets.role: crop descriptor scores for fruit, flower, leaf, and other organs across accessions

candidate_datasets.name: Genesys
candidate_datasets.role: passport and characterization data for genebank accessions of cultivated plants

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: continuous leaf and other functional traits for a subset of crops and landraces

obstacles: Genebank descriptors are often categorical, missing, and not measured with a common protocol.
Correlation of growth predicts that selected organs will drag others along, which shrinks the expected contrast.
The identity of the historically selected organ is uncertain for many old landraces.
assessments.rationale: Descriptor databases for cultivated plants contain the organ-level variables for a direct variance partition in major crops. Coverage and measurement quality fall off outside those crops, and correlated change is both a biological fact and a confounder of this particular contrast. A small team could run the test for well-described crops and would be extrapolating to cultivated plants as a whole.

assessments.operationalization: Track phenotypic or breeding-value change in populations where the recorded practice was only 'breed from the best animals' without a written improvement target, over multi-decade to century scales, and compare the direction of change with methodical breeding programmes. Sustained change in the preferred direction under the weaker practice would support the claim; stasis once methodical goals are absent would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Domestic Animal Diversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: breed identity and coarse status over recent decades, not century-scale unconscious selection

candidate_datasets.name: USDA GRIN
candidate_datasets.role: landrace accessions that preserve older cultivated stocks for a static comparison

obstacles: Historical records rarely label a breeding practice as unconscious rather than methodical.
Nutrition, climate, and market standards change the phenotype in parallel with any breeding choice.
Open breed databases do not store century-long individual pedigrees tied to selection criteria.
assessments.rationale: The process can be approximated with long phenotypic series under weak selection, but public breed systems do not encode intent or century-scale pedigrees. Landrace collections and breed lists support only a static proxy. Environment and methodical selection remain tangled with any trend that can be assembled from papers and herd books.

assessments.operationalization: For plants with the longest cultivation histories, score whether a wild progenitor is identified and measure genomic or phenotypic distance to the nearest wild relative. The explanatory claim would be supported if unidentified progenitors were exactly the most diverged stocks; it would be weakened if large divergence still left progenitors identifiable, or if unidentified parents were mostly extinct or unsampled rather than unrecognizably modified.

candidate_datasets.name: USDA GRIN
candidate_datasets.role: crop wild-relative classification and accession records linking crops to progenitors

candidate_datasets.name: Genesys
candidate_datasets.role: genebank holdings of crops and wild relatives used to judge whether parents are known and sampled

candidate_datasets.name: World Flora Online
candidate_datasets.role: accepted names and taxonomy for cultivated species and candidate wild parents

obstacles: A wild parent may be unrecognizable because it is extinct or uncollected, not because the crop changed.
Hybrid origins create several partial parents rather than one unrecognizable stock.
Minor garden plants are far less completely linked to wild relatives than major staples.
assessments.rationale: Crop wild-relative databases and floras now record progenitor status for a large set of long-cultivated plants, and sequence archives can supply distances for the staples. That is enough to test recognizability as a present-day fact and to compare it with divergence for well-studied crops. Extinction, hybridization, and thin coverage of ornamental garden plants keep the causal story, accumulated change as the reason parents are unknown, only partly identified.

assessments.operationalization: Partition multivariate disparity among breeds into external characters and internal organs, using size-corrected measurements from the same individuals. Greater external disparity would support the contrast; equal or greater internal disparity would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT and surface scans that can include both external shape and internal skeletons for some domestic breeds

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: specimen index for locating comparative anatomical series of domestic races

obstacles: Few breeds have both external and internal measurements on a common sample.
Allometry and body-size divergence move internal organs without any direct selection on them.
Soft organs are rarely preserved in the scan collections that are public.
assessments.rationale: The external-versus-internal partition is straightforward wherever both are measured, and 3D archives contain pieces of it for dogs and a few other animals. They are not a designed comparative sample of domestic races, and soft anatomy is largely missing. A result for skulls and limb bones would be a restricted proxy for the full contrast.

assessments.operationalization: Relate the rate at which useful or selected variants appear, or the rate of genetic gain, to the number of individuals kept, holding heritability and generation interval fixed. A strong positive partial association would support the importance of numbers; no association once effort and heritability are controlled would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Domestic Animal Diversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: breed-level population sizes, without rates of appearance of useful variants

candidate_datasets.name: European Variation Archive
candidate_datasets.role: counts of rare variants as a function of how many individuals were sequenced, a sampling proxy

obstacles: Once useful variants are assumed to be rare and random, a larger herd raising the chance they appear is close to a sampling identity.
Breeding-programme gain, census size, and investment are rarely public in the same table and are strongly confounded.
Sequencing depth is not the same variable as the number of animals a breeder keeps.
assessments.rationale: Population-size catalogues and variant archives proxy the sampling half of the statement for a few domestic species. They do not record the appearance of variations that breeders find useful, which is the outcome that would have to be compared with other ingredients of success. The testable residue is a confounded correlation between herd size and gain, not a clean ranking of causes.

assessments.operationalization: Decompose among-breed phenotypic and genomic differences into components attributable to selection response, direct environmental effects, correlated response, and hybrid ancestry. Selection would be the predominant power if its component exceeded the sum of the others across a representative set of races; a larger share for conditions, use, correlation, or crossing would count against that ranking.

candidate_datasets.name: European Variation Archive
candidate_datasets.role: breed differentiation and selected sweeps in sequenced livestock

candidate_datasets.name: Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals
candidate_datasets.role: known selected loci versus syndromes that track use, disease, or correlated defects

candidate_datasets.name: USDA GRIN
candidate_datasets.role: crop accession phenotypes where selection history and pedigree are partly documented

obstacles: There is no agreed scale on which to add 'power' across selection, climate, use, correlation, and crossing.
Selection scans detect some selected loci and miss polygenic and environmental change.
Plastic responses to rearing conditions are rarely measured in the same animals as breed genomics.
assessments.rationale: Genomic differentiation and crop evaluation data can show that selection has left a large mark on major domestic races, which addresses only part of a ranking among causes. The other causes are poorly collocated in the same records, so the predominance claim stays under-identified. Several decompositions are possible, and any one of them would take substantial harmonization for a handful of species.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate heritability of ordinary within-species individual differences and the response to selection on those differences, as opposed to responses that require rare sports or new mutations. Positive heritability and a response attributable to standing individual differences would support the claim; evolution that proceeds only by rare macromutations, or individual differences that are never heritable, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Barcode of Life Data Systems
candidate_datasets.role: within-species sequence variation as a widespread record of individual differences

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: population-level sequences showing standing variation available to selection

obstacles: Sequence differences are a reinterpretation of the visible individual differences Darwin treated as the raw material.
Heritability and selection response are scattered across studies and are not columns in the barcode archives.
The statement is close to the definition of selection on standing variation once heritability is granted.
assessments.rationale: Barcode and sequence archives document that individuals of a species differ, for a wide taxonomic range, and a smaller literature shows those differences are often heritable. The archives themselves do not contain the selection-response test, so the mechanism is only partly in existing open tables. A result would speak to a well-studied subset and would still sit close to the definition of selection on standing variation.

assessments.operationalization: Within polymorphic genera such as Rubus, Rosa, and Hieracium, compare selection gradients or functional effects of characters that vary excessively with characters that are stable. The suspicion would be supported if the variable characters had gradients indistinguishable from zero while stable characters did not; strong selection on the variable characters would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: trait measurements for genera that include apomictic and polymorphic groups

candidate_datasets.name: World Flora Online
candidate_datasets.role: species lists and synonymy indicating which genera are taxonomically unstable

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: regional floras that record variable species complexes

obstacles: Inferring that a character is useless because it is unfixed makes the test circular.
Selection gradients for Rubus, Rosa, and Hieracium are not compiled in an open trait database.
Apomixis and taxonomic oversplitting create polymorphism that has nothing to do with the selective value of a structure.
assessments.rationale: Floras and trait databases can show which groups and characters are polymorphic. They do not contain an independent measure of service or disservice, so the selective explanation is weakly identified. A non-circular test would need fitness data that are still study-specific and taxonomically narrow.

assessments.operationalization: Score taxa whose rank is disputed between species and variety, restrict the set to highly mobile animals that mate to reproduce, and compare how often those forms are sympatric within one country versus allopatric across separated areas. The pattern would be supported if doubtful forms were disproportionately allopatric in that group relative to sessile organisms; a similar rate of sympatric doubtful forms would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: BirdLife Data Zone
candidate_datasets.role: bird range maps and taxonomic treatments for sympatry versus allopatry of close forms

candidate_datasets.name: Map of Life
candidate_datasets.role: range products across animal groups for co-occurrence within countries

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: species and infraspecific names used to flag forms of uncertain rank

obstacles: 'Doubtful' is a property of taxonomic disagreement, which tracks how thoroughly a group has been studied.
Birds are well mapped and insects are not, so the mobile-animal scope is unevenly covered.
Political borders are an imperfect stand-in for Darwin's 'same country'.
assessments.rationale: Range products and checklists make a sympatry-versus-allopatry test practical for birds and some other mobile vertebrates. Doubtful rank has to be proxied by subspecies status or checklist conflict, and insects remain thinly and unevenly digitized. Sampling effort and taxonomic fashion can create the geographic pattern, so the result would be informative with a serious bias correction rather than decisive on its own.

assessments.operationalization: Build distributions of genetic and phenotypic distance for pairs ranked as individual variants, varieties, subspecies, and species. A single overlapping continuum would support the absence of a clear line; a repeatable gap between adjacent ranks, stable across groups, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Barcode of Life Data Systems
candidate_datasets.role: within- and between-species genetic distances for millions of animal specimens

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: additional loci and plant sequences where barcodes are sparse

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: rank labels (species, subspecies, variety) attached to the names being compared

obstacles: Barcode libraries sample species much more densely than the variety-to-individual end of the series.
A gap in animals can coexist with overlap in plants, so the universal wording can fail in one kingdom and hold in another.
Rank labels are partly conventional, so the test recycles taxonomic practice unless distances are computed first and ranks applied after.
assessments.rationale: Public barcodes, sequences, and rank catalogues already support a distance-continuum test that many groups have effectively received. Adequacy is high for animal species boundaries and weaker for plants and for the fine end of individual differences, which is part of the stated series. The analysis is standard, and the main limit is that a gap at one rank in one kingdom would refute the fully universal reading without settling every taxon.

assessments.operationalization: Along phylogeographic series, test whether populations ranked as slight varieties, marked varieties, and species differ by increasing, directionally selected trait change rather than by drift-sized divergence. A graded series whose steps are enriched for selected loci would support natural selection as the main passage; series produced by isolation and drift alone would count against that attribution.

candidate_datasets.name: Barcode of Life Data Systems
candidate_datasets.role: population and species clusters used as a proxy for varieties and incipient species

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: placement of close relatives on phylogenies

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: multilocus data for divergence and selection scans in well-studied complexes

obstacles: 'Incipient species' and 'definite directions' need a threshold that is not in the original wording.
Drift, founder events, and selection all produce stepped divergence.
Selection scans and variety ranks are rarely in the same public table outside a few model complexes.
assessments.rationale: Sequence and tree archives can line up close forms into a divergence series, which proxies the descriptive half. They seldom include the fitness or selection measures needed to show that natural selection, rather than drift, accumulates the steps. The mechanistic ranking is therefore only partly testable, and only in complexes that happen to have both ranks and population genomics.

assessments.operationalization: Treat 'no essential difference' as overlap between the divergence, reproductive isolation, and phylogenetic depth of sets named as species and sets named as varieties, and treat 'arbitrary' as inter-author discordance in rank for the same populations. A unique biological gap that taxonomists recover repeatedly would count against the statement; overlapping distributions and unstable ranks would support the empirical reading.

candidate_datasets.name: Barcode of Life Data Systems
candidate_datasets.role: genetic distances across names ranked as species and as infraspecific forms

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: current rank assignments whose stability and cutoffs can be compared

candidate_datasets.name: World Flora Online
candidate_datasets.role: botanical species and variety names, where the variety rank remains in use

obstacles: 'Essentially' and 'for convenience' are philosophical even after a biological gap is defined.
Different species concepts predict different gaps, so several operationalizations compete.
Discordance among checklists measures nomenclatural practice as much as biology.
assessments.rationale: The wording is partly about how a term is used, and that part does not pick out a single measurement. The biological reading, that species and varieties are not different in kind, can be proxied with public distances and ranks and has the same limits as a continuum test. Competing species concepts keep any one gap from settling the essentialist contrast, which is why discriminating power stays modest.

assessments.operationalization: Regress the number of well-marked varieties per species on geographic range, local occupancy, and abundance, within regional floras, with sampling effort as a covariate. A positive partial association for wide, common species would support the pattern; no association after effort is controlled would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Botanical Information and Ecology Network
candidate_datasets.role: plant occurrence, range, and abundance-related plot data

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: regional floras that list species and, unevenly, infraspecific taxa

candidate_datasets.name: Map of Life
candidate_datasets.role: range and occupancy surfaces used to score dominance

obstacles: Widespread species are collected and split more often, which manufactures varieties.
Abundance, range, and 'variety' rank are complete together only for some regional floras.
Darwin's dominance criteria (world range, local diffusion, and numbers) are only partly observed in the same records.
assessments.rationale: Range, plot, and flora databases contain the dominance variables and at least partial variety counts for plants, which is the stated scope. The classic sampling bias, that common plants attract more taxonomic attention, is large enough that an uncorrected regression would not discriminate the biological claim. A careful subset analysis is feasible; a global, bias-resistant one is not sitting ready to run.

assessments.operationalization: Within each country or regional biota, compare the proportion of species that have named varieties, and the mean number of varieties, between species in genera above and below the median genus size. Higher proportions and means on the large-genus side, after controlling for study effort, would support the pattern; a null or reversed difference would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: World Flora Online
candidate_datasets.role: genus sizes and infraspecific names for plants

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: country and regional floras matching Darwin's within-country comparison

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: genus membership and variety counts, including some animal groups such as beetles where digitized

obstacles: Variety rank is used inconsistently and is often omitted from global checklists.
Large genera are studied more intensively, so they accumulate more named varieties.
Beetle faunas, part of the original scope, are less consistently digitized than vascular-plant floras.
assessments.rationale: The comparison is a direct contingency table of genus size against variety counts, and floras plus name catalogues supply it for many countries' plants. Infraspecific ranks are incomplete and effort-biased, so discriminating power sits at the level of a correctable confound rather than a clean test. Animal groups in the original scope would need extra compilation beyond the plant floras.

assessments.operationalization: From occurrence counts in time bins, reconstruct genus-richness trajectories and estimate how often small genera later become much richer and how often rich genera peak, decline, and disappear. Those two frequencies being high, after sampling standardization, would support the geological generalization; trajectories dominated by flat or monotonically biased richness would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: genus occurrences by time bin for richness trajectories

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: stable marine genus names to reduce taxonomic inflation in the best-sampled fossil groups

obstacles: Uncorrected richness rises toward the present because of rock area and preservation, independent of true diversification.
Last occurrences are smeared backward by incomplete sampling.
Shelly marine animals dominate the usable record, so plants and terrestrial genera are a biased remainder.
assessments.rationale: The Paleobiology Database is built for exactly this richness-through-time question, and a standardized analysis is routine for a small team. What it can resolve well is the marine shelly subset, not genera in the fossil record as a whole. Sampling and preservation biases are serious enough that raw peaks and declines are only partly informative, even though the direction of a corrected test is clear.

assessments.operationalization: Compare recent speciation rates, or counts of subspecies and phylogeographic splits, with present genus richness. A positive average relationship would support the prediction that where many species have formed, many are still forming; no relationship, or a negative one, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenies for tip rates and clade richness

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: divergence times used to score recent versus ancient splitting

candidate_datasets.name: BirdTree
candidate_datasets.role: a densely sampled clade in which recent speciation and genus size can be compared

obstacles: Tip-rate estimators are biased by tree shape, sampling fraction, and taxonomic splitting.
Subspecies counts repeat the effort bias that affects variety counts.
A large genus can be old and slow, which satisfies 'many have formed' without 'many are still forming'.
assessments.rationale: Dated trees make a richness-versus-recent-speciation regression possible for vertebrates and some plants. The prediction is close to a measurable variable, but rate artifacts and uneven species sampling are large. The test is a real one for well-sampled clades and a proxy for genera of plants and animals in general.

assessments.operationalization: Regress mean pairwise morphological or genetic distance among congeners on genus richness. Smaller distances in larger genera would support the pattern; equal or larger distances would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: within-genus phylogenetic distances as one measure of amount of difference

candidate_datasets.name: Barcode of Life Data Systems
candidate_datasets.role: pairwise genetic distances among congeners, especially insects

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: morphological trait distances among plant congeners where species means exist

obstacles: Taxonomists split large genera more finely, which shrinks genetic distances by practice.
Trait databases often store one mean per species and miss the characters Darwin compared.
Phylogenetic distance and morphological difference can disagree about which genera are 'close'.
assessments.rationale: Pairwise distances and genus sizes are both in open trees, barcode libraries, and, more patchily, trait tables. A negative relationship is directly computable for insects and many plant genera. Because small gaps are partly how large genera get delimited, morphology is the less circular measure and it is the less complete dataset, so the test remains only partly discriminating.

assessments.operationalization: Measure clustering of species around a few centers inside large genera, using morphological nearest-neighbour structure or phylogenetic satellites around paraphyletic nominal species, and compare that clustering with a constant-rate branching null. Excess clustering around a few species would support the satellite pattern; distances as even as the null would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: within-genus tree shape for uneven clustering

candidate_datasets.name: BirdTree
candidate_datasets.role: complete avian trees for a null-model comparison in one large clade

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: trait-space clustering of plant species within large genera

obstacles: Ordinary branching processes already produce clusters, so the null has to be explicit.
Satellite species around a still-living 'parent' require paraphyletic species concepts that many trees have already removed.
Morphological clustering and phylogenetic clustering answer different versions of the statement.
assessments.rationale: Trees and trait tables can show uneven spacing inside large genera for well-sampled groups. The specific picture of satellites around certain species is stricter than generic tree imbalance, and standard phylogenies often erase the paraphyly that picture needs. The analysis is feasible and only moderately discriminating once a branching null is included.

assessments.operationalization: Regress geographic range size on distance to the nearest congener, phylogenetically or morphologically defined. Smaller ranges for the closest species would support the pattern; no relationship, or larger ranges for the closest species, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Map of Life
candidate_datasets.role: geographic ranges for species whose nearest relatives can be identified

candidate_datasets.name: BirdLife Data Zone
candidate_datasets.role: expert bird range polygons, less occurrence-biased than raw records

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: nearest-relative distances within genera

obstacles: Recently described close species are often known from few localities, which shrinks apparent range.
Occurrence-based ranges under-represent poorly sampled regions and narrow endemics differently.
Young species may have small ranges because they are young, which is related to the claim but not identical to a variety-like restriction.
assessments.rationale: Range surfaces and phylogenies make this regression a standard macroecological test for birds, mammals, and many plants. Adequacy is that of well-mapped groups rather than species generally, matching a claim that started from the British flora and was generalized. Description bias and age-range correlations are serious, and they are quantifiable, so the result can be informative without being fully clean.

assessments.operationalization: Test the bundle of variety-like statistics for species in large genera (more infraspecific forms, small unequal gaps, restricted ranges of close allies) and ask whether that bundle is predicted by descent of species from varieties. Failure of the bundle would undermine the explanatory claim; success would favour descent only relative to a creation hypothesis that forbids variety-like structure.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: relatedness structure against which variety-like species patterns are scored

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: flora-level variety and range patterns that form the analogies

candidate_datasets.name: Map of Life
candidate_datasets.role: range sizes of close species, one of the analogies in the bundle

obstacles: Independent creation can be adjusted to produce any observed pattern, so confirmation is weak.
The analogies are the same facts used in the neighbouring variety-and-genus claims, and a joint test double-counts them.
Descent predicts the bundle only after extra assumptions about rates and extinction.
assessments.rationale: The component patterns can be measured with trees, floras, and ranges, so the factual bundle is partly open to analysis. The contrast with independent creation is poorly discriminating because that rival does not forbid a specific outcome. A missing bundle would hurt the argument, while a present bundle would still be compatible with more than one historical story.

assessments.operationalization: Test whether larger genera tend to gain species through time more than smaller ones, and whether species that are widespread and abundant leave more descendant species that are themselves widespread. A positive richness trend and a positive descendant-dominance relationship, above a passive-diffusion null, would support the prediction; large genera shrinking as often as they grow, or dominant species leaving no more dominant descendants, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: genus-size changes through time

candidate_datasets.name: Map of Life
candidate_datasets.role: present dominance measured as range, an imperfect stand-in for ancestral dominance

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: descendant counts of living clades that are currently dominant

obstacles: Large genera are expected to wander more under a passive null, so growth is not automatically a driven trend.
Abundance and dominance of ancestors are barely preserved, so descendant dominance is proxied by living range.
Extant trees lack the failed lineages that would have made dominant groups look less inevitably successful.
assessments.rationale: Fossil richness trajectories and living ranges can test pieces of a tendency for large and dominant groups to expand. Ancestral dominance and 'modified dominant descendants' are not directly in those tables, so the second half is a proxy. Passive statistical trends and missing extinct side-branches keep a positive pattern from isolating the stated mechanism.

assessments.operationalization: Compare potential population growth at low density, from fecundity and survival schedules, with realized long-term abundance. Potential growth well above replacement, with realized numbers checked by conspecifics, other species, or physical factors, would support the argument; life histories whose maximum growth is at or below replacement would refute universal geometrical overproduction.

candidate_datasets.name: COMPADRE and COMADRE
candidate_datasets.role: matrix models giving potential growth, fecundity, and survival

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fecundity and growth parameters for a species-rich animal group

candidate_datasets.name: Living Planet Index
candidate_datasets.role: realized abundance time series that stay far below unbounded increase

obstacles: The struggle is said to be with conspecifics, other species, or physical conditions, a disjunction that covers every possible check.
Demographic matrices are biased toward plants, vertebrates, and temperate studies.
Potential growth estimated from a short study can misrepresent the long-run tendency to increase.
assessments.rationale: Open matrix-population and abundance databases can test geometrical potential versus realized numbers for hundreds of species, and the calculation is standard. The universal scope is only sampled, and the tripartite 'struggle' is hard to refute because every limit falls into one of the three bins. The resolvable part is overproduction, not the exhaustive classification of checks.

assessments.operationalization: Compare fecundity of species in native versus introduced ranges, and compare survival or population growth over the same contrast, for naturalized plants and animals. Rapid spread with unchanged fecundity and higher survival would support geometrical increase under lower mortality; a systematic rise in fertility sufficient to explain the increase would count against the stated mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Naturalized Alien Flora
candidate_datasets.role: which plants are naturalized where, the spread outcome for floras

candidate_datasets.name: COMPADRE and COMADRE
candidate_datasets.role: vital rates for some invasive and native populations

candidate_datasets.name: Map of Life
candidate_datasets.role: occupied range of introduced species as a measure of spread

obstacles: Vital-rate comparisons in both ranges exist for far fewer species than naturalization records.
Evolved increases in fecundity and enemy-release effects on body size can raise fertility after introduction.
GloNAF covers plants, while the statement also includes animals.
assessments.rationale: Naturalization inventories and range products document rapid spread, and demographic matrices contain the fecundity-versus-survival contrast for a subset. The mechanism is testable where both ranges have vital rates and is only inferred from occurrence elsewhere. Animal invasions and evolved fertility changes keep the full statement partly unresolved.

assessments.operationalization: In a phylogenetic regression, predict average abundance from fecundity after controlling for juvenile survival and body size. A weak partial effect of fecundity, together with a positive association between fecundity and early mortality, would support indirect dependence and compensation; a strong direct fecundity-abundance relationship with no early-mortality tradeoff would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: COMPADRE and COMADRE
candidate_datasets.role: fecundity and age-specific survival, including early mortality

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fecundity, length, and resilience or abundance fields for fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Living Planet Index
candidate_datasets.role: relative abundance for species that also have life-history records

obstacles: Body size drives both fecundity and abundance and must be partialled out.
Absolute average abundance is missing for many species that have excellent fecundity data.
The joint sample is biased toward well-studied vertebrates, fish, and plants.
assessments.rationale: Fecundity, survival, and at least relative abundance are public for a large comparative sample, and the regression is a standard life-history test. The sample is still a subset of animals and plants, and size confounding is serious though tractable. The statement is close to resolvable for that subset and not yet a full-scope census.

assessments.operationalization: Compare effect sizes of predator removal and of food supplementation on equilibrium density across field experiments. Predation determining average numbers 'very frequently' would be supported if predator treatments changed density more often, or by more, than food treatments, while food still set an upper bound in enrichment studies; the reverse pattern would count against the frequency claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Nutrient Network
candidate_datasets.role: standardized nutrient (food) additions and plant-density responses

candidate_datasets.name: LTER Network
candidate_datasets.role: long-term site data, some with both consumer and resource manipulations

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: trophic level and population-biology fields for fishes where predation and food are both discussed

obstacles: Predator-exclusion results are scattered across papers rather than one open experiment archive.
Food and predation interact, and short experiments miss the upper food limit.
Nutrient-network data cover plants, whereas the clearest predation claim is about animals.
assessments.rationale: The contrast between predator and food effects is operationally clear and has been meta-analysed in the literature, but the public experimental tables are incomplete. Nutrient-addition data are the strongest open piece and address only the food side, mostly for plants. A frequency judgment of 'very often' across animal populations would require compiling a biased, study-level sample.

assessments.operationalization: Attribute interannual changes in abundance to extreme cold or drought versus predation, disease, food, and competition, using a common mortality or growth currency. Climate extremes would be the most effective check if their standardized effects exceeded the others across species; comparable or larger biotic effects would refute the superlative.

candidate_datasets.name: Living Planet Index
candidate_datasets.role: abundance time series that can be aligned with climate anomalies

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: temperature and precipitation extremes as candidate checks

candidate_datasets.name: LTER Network
candidate_datasets.role: site time series where causes of population change are sometimes identified

obstacles: Most abundance series lack a cause-of-death field, so climate correlations are not a comparison among all checks.
Extremes are confounded with food shortage and predator success in the same season.
'Most effective of all checks' needs a shared unit that different studies do not use.
assessments.rationale: Population indices and climate layers can test whether bad years track cold and drought for well-monitored species. They cannot, by themselves, rank climate against predation, disease, and competition. The superlative is only partly approachable with long-term sites where causes were recorded, and that subset is small.

assessments.operationalization: Measure species richness along latitude and elevation, and measure the frequency of stunted individuals, asking whether stunting tracks direct climate stress more strongly poleward and uphill than equatorward and downhill, after accounting for season length and soil. A steeper richness decline and a higher share of climate-limited stunting toward the poles and summits would support the statement; stunting that is equally common in benign climates, or richness that does not decline, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Botanical Information and Ecology Network
candidate_datasets.role: plant occurrences and plot composition along latitude and elevation

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: temperature and precipitation surfaces for the climate gradient

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: plant height and size traits used to score stunting

obstacles: Short stature can be an adaptation to season length or nutrients rather than direct climatic injury.
Richness declines are real and still have many causes, so they do not by themselves show fewer competitors.
Tropical and high-elevation plot coverage is uneven, which can exaggerate apparent stunting.
assessments.rationale: Richness and plant-size gradients are directly in open occurrence, climate, and trait databases, and the geographic pattern is analyzable now for plants. The claim also says the stunting is caused by direct climate injury because competitors drop out, and height data do not identify that mechanism. Discriminating power is limited to the pattern plus a weak proxy for the cause.

assessments.operationalization: Compare climate tolerance of cultivated exotic plants with whether they are naturalized, and relate naturalization failure to competitive and enemy-related traits rather than to hardiness. A large set of climate-hardy non-naturalized plants, with naturalization predicted by biotic traits, would support indirect climatic limitation; naturalization predicted by climate tolerance alone would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Naturalized Alien Flora
candidate_datasets.role: naturalization status of plant species by region

candidate_datasets.name: USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map
candidate_datasets.role: climate-tolerance geography for cultivated plants

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: competitive and defence traits of exotic and native plants

obstacles: Garden hardiness and naturalization status are easy to join for some regions and messy for others.
Failure to naturalize can reflect propagule pressure and habitat availability, not only competitors and native animals.
The garden-plant example is narrower than 'climate limits species mainly indirectly' for all species.
assessments.rationale: Naturalization inventories, hardiness geography, and traits can test Darwin's garden argument for plants in well-documented regions. That is a restricted and reasonably direct test of indirect limitation. Extending 'mainly' to species in general, and separating competition from propagule pressure, exceeds what those tables cleanly support.

assessments.operationalization: Test for positive density dependence at low density in demographic models, and test whether geographically rare plants are locally abundant where they occur, relative to their enemies' density. Allee effects plus locally high density of range-restricted plants would support the statement; strictly negative density dependence and rare plants that are also locally sparse would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Botanical Information and Ecology Network
candidate_datasets.role: local abundance and geographic occurrence of plant species

candidate_datasets.name: sPlot
candidate_datasets.role: vegetation plots for local density of narrow-ranging species

candidate_datasets.name: COMPADRE and COMADRE
candidate_datasets.role: density-dependent demographic models where Allee effects can be flagged

obstacles: Local abundance of rare plants can reflect habitat specialization rather than swamping of enemies.
Enemy density is rarely recorded in the same plots as the plant census.
Most matrix models are not density-dependent, so Allee effects are a small, biased subset.
assessments.rationale: Plot databases can test the biogeographic pattern that some rare plants are locally numerous, and a few demographic models speak to Allee effects. Enemy-relative stock size, which is the mechanism, is usually missing. The result can support or weaken the pattern for plants and only proxy the survival rule.

assessments.operationalization: Quantify temporal turnover in community composition over long monitoring series, and, where perturbations exist, estimate how small a change shifts dominance. Long periods of low turnover would support uniformity; high sensitivity to small pushes would support the tipping clause; a series cannot support both clauses unless stability and sensitivity are given separate thresholds.

candidate_datasets.name: BioTIME
candidate_datasets.role: assemblage time series for compositional uniformity

candidate_datasets.name: LTER Network
candidate_datasets.role: decadal community data and some experimental perturbations

candidate_datasets.name: sPlot
candidate_datasets.role: resurveyed vegetation plots as a spatial-temporal complement

obstacles: The statement combines long-run uniformity with hair-trigger sensitivity, which need different designs.
Most series span years to decades, not the long periods implied, and coarse taxonomy inflates apparent stability.
Apparent turnover is confounded with sampling error and observer change.
assessments.rationale: Community time-series archives can measure whether composition stays similar, which is half the statement and is already a standard analysis. They rarely include the trifling perturbation that would show the balance is easy to tip. Short duration, sampling noise, and the tension between the two halves keep the full wording only partly testable.

assessments.operationalization: Trace indirect paths in interaction networks and, where abundance data exist, estimate whether changing one species' abundance predicts another's through an intermediate. Documented indirect effects would support the possibility of such chains; a systematic absence of indirect paths from predators to plants via seed predators or pollinators would count against the general mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: species-interaction records from which multi-step chains can be built

candidate_datasets.name: Web of Life
candidate_datasets.role: ecological networks with quantitative links for a subset of communities

obstacles: Most interaction records are presence of a link, not an effect on abundance.
A chain that is possible on a graph may be dynamically unimportant.
The cat-mouse-bee-clover example is more specific than the global interaction tables can reconstruct for one district.
assessments.rationale: Open interaction networks can show multi-step links among dissimilar organisms, which supports the existential reading that abundance effects can travel through intermediates. Quantitative frequency control is present in only a minority of networks. The analysis is feasible for well-resolved webs and does not cover terrestrial communities at the scope of the example.

assessments.operationalization: Compare the strength of intraspecific competition with interspecific competition, using per-capita effects from removal experiments, frequency dependence, or fitted competition coefficients. A general ranking of intraspecific effects as stronger, including among varieties, would support the statement; interspecific effects as strong or stronger in most pairs would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Nutrient Network
candidate_datasets.role: plant community responses that can separate conspecific density from neighborhood diversity

candidate_datasets.name: sPlot
candidate_datasets.role: local co-occurrence and abundance for estimating competition proxies in vegetation

candidate_datasets.name: COMPADRE and COMADRE
candidate_datasets.role: demographic density dependence, sometimes attributable to conspecific crowding

obstacles: Direct competition coefficients are compiled in papers more than in one open database.
Co-occurrence is a poor proxy for the severity of a struggle.
Varieties of domesticated organisms, included in the scope, are rarely in the same competition datasets as wild species.
assessments.rationale: Intraspecific versus interspecific effect size is a standard and discriminating contrast, and plant-community datasets plus demographic models cover a real subset. The cleanest coefficients are still scattered, so a global 'almost always' ranking would mean harmonizing studies for weeks to months. Animals and domesticated varieties are the thin part of the scope.

assessments.operationalization: Compare competition coefficients, or naturalization and co-occurrence outcomes, for congeners versus species in different genera, controlling for habitat overlap. Stronger negative effects among congeners would support the statement; equal or weaker congener effects would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Naturalized Alien Flora
candidate_datasets.role: naturalization success in the presence of congeneric natives, a standard proxy

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: genus membership and relatedness of co-occurring species

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: regional species lists for congener versus non-congener co-occurrence

obstacles: Relatedness is an imperfect proxy for similarity of habits, so genus rank can miss the real competitors.
Habitat filtering makes close relatives co-occur, which looks like weak competition.
Experimental competition coefficients between congeners are far fewer than co-occurrence records.
assessments.rationale: Naturalization and co-occurrence tests of congener competition are doable with open flora, tree, and alien-plant data, especially for plants. Those tests proxy severity rather than measuring it, and habitat filtering can reverse the sign.
