The analysis is standard for floras and only partly adequate for animals and for true competition coefficients.

assessments.operationalization: Ask what fraction of measured structures are statistically predictable from the traits of competitors, predators, prey, or escape targets, against a phylogeny-and-environment null. A large excess of matched structures would support pervasive relatedness of form; a null match rate would challenge the universal reading only for relations that are visible in the data.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: who competes, eats, or is eaten by whom

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: plant structures to compare with interaction partners

candidate_datasets.name: Web of Life
candidate_datasets.role: network context for trait matching in a subset of communities

obstacles: Relations that are 'often hidden' can be postulated whenever a test finds no match, which blocks refutation.
'Every' organism and 'essential' relation have no natural numerical threshold.
Trait matching often restates known natural history (bill and prey size) for a few well-studied guilds.
assessments.rationale: Interaction archives and trait databases can test visible matching between structures and partners for a biased but real subset of organisms. The universal and 'hidden' wording survives a null result, so discriminating power is low. What existing data can resolve is a proxy: whether known interactions predict form better than environment and phylogeny alone, in guilds that have both traits and links.

assessments.operationalization: For each species, compare the climate at documented range edges with laboratory thermal limits and with the ranges of co-occurring species. The claim would be confirmed if only a small minority of edges sit at physiological tolerance limits and most edges lie inside the fundamental niche where other species turn over; it would be refuted if a large fraction of edges coincide with tolerance limits in regions with no plausible competitor.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: georeferenced occurrences used to locate range edges

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: climate surfaces at range edges

candidate_datasets.name: GlobTherm
candidate_datasets.role: measured thermal tolerances for comparing fundamental and realized limits

obstacles: Thermal-tolerance measurements cover a biased minority of species, mostly ectotherms.
A climatic edge can reflect dispersal failure or an unmeasured interaction rather than death from climate.
Competitor identity is rarely recorded at the same edges as climate and physiology.
assessments.rationale: Range edges, climate, and thermal limits are standard variables, and the decision rule is a fraction of species whose edges match physiological limits. Public databases contain those variables directly, but physiological coverage is too thin for plants, endotherms, and most insects, and biotic data are sparser still. Occurrence models also confound climate with history and source-sink dynamics, so a global test would speak clearly only for the better-measured subset.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate the distribution of fitness effects from allele-frequency spectra, and estimate surplus offspring from life tables. Purifying selection would be confirmed if deleterious alleles are systematically rarer than neutral alleles and if populations produce far more offspring than survive; the differential-success clause would be refuted if fitness effects did not predict frequency change. The sentence that names this process natural selection has no separate measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: gnomAD
candidate_datasets.role: human allele frequencies and constraint metrics for deleterious variants

candidate_datasets.name: COMPADRE & COMADRE
candidate_datasets.role: stage-structured fecundity and survival matrices for plants and animals

candidate_datasets.name: LTEE
candidate_datasets.role: frequency trajectories of mutations with small fitness effects in experimental E. coli

obstacles: An advantage defined as higher survival or reproduction makes the central clause close to a definition of fitness.
Population-genomic samples are concentrated in humans and model organisms.
Life tables show excess births without identifying which heritable differences selection retains.
assessments.rationale: Superfecundity and the removal of deleterious alleles are measurable, and open demographic and genomic resources support standard tests of both. The preservation of favourable variation is only weakly separable from the definition of a favourable variant, so many outcomes are compatible with the wording either as a mechanism or as a tautology. Existing data therefore test pieces of the statement in a few well-studied organisms rather than the universal process as named.

assessments.operationalization: Classify variants by an independent fitness assay or functional annotation, then compare their heterozygosity and time spent polymorphic with neutral expectations. The claim would be confirmed if alleles with no detectable fitness effect persist as a fluctuating component while selected alleles do not, including in species long called polymorphic; it would be refuted if persistent polymorphisms are predominantly maintained by balancing selection.

candidate_datasets.name: gnomAD
candidate_datasets.role: site-frequency spectra and constraint for separating neutral from selected variants

candidate_datasets.name: 1000 Genomes Project
candidate_datasets.role: population polymorphism data for allele-frequency dynamics

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: population-genomic sequences for non-human species

obstacles: Balancing selection keeps variation that is useful under some conditions, which the neutral wording does not separate cleanly.
Nineteenth-century polymorphic species are not a standardized trait class in modern databases.
Phenotypic polymorphism data are scattered relative to sequence polymorphism.
assessments.rationale: Sequence polymorphism and fitness annotations are public and the site-frequency spectrum is a standard discriminator of neutral and selected alleles. That test covers a modest set of taxa and mostly nucleotide variants rather than the visible polymorphisms Darwin had in mind. Balancing selection is a serious alternative route to long-lived polymorphism, so the analysis is informative for sequence evolution and only a proxy for polymorphic species.

assessments.operationalization: For each country or flora, count established non-native species and the fraction of the biota they represent. Universal establishment would confirm the naturalisation pattern Darwin treats as evidence; absence of established non-natives from many regions would refute that pattern. Establishment itself would not confirm that native populations could have been improved by selection, because enemy release and disturbance produce the same invasions.

candidate_datasets.name: GloNAF
candidate_datasets.role: regional lists of naturalized alien plants

candidate_datasets.name: Global Invasive Species Database
candidate_datasets.role: established non-native species, including animals, by region

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence evidence that non-native taxa persist in each country

obstacles: Invasion success also follows propagule pressure, disturbance, and release from enemies.
Animal naturalizations are less completely tabulated than plants.
Firm possession is a qualitative threshold that checklists do not measure directly.
assessments.rationale: Whether non-native species have established in every country is a direct count, and global plant inventories already support it at high coverage. The further inference, that natives were therefore imperfectly adapted and could be improved, is not identified by establishment: several ecological alternatives predict the same lists. A small team could settle the biogeographic pattern quickly and would still lack a clean test of perfect adaptation.

assessments.operationalization: Score prey colour against the background where the animal is found, and compare attack rates on matching and mismatched forms by visually hunting predators. Higher survival of matching forms would confirm a protective effect of the tint; equal survival after accounting for temperature and sexual signalling would refute it. Open photo and specimen archives support the match, while the survival contrast lives mainly in individual experiments.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: photographs linking organism colour to the immediate background

candidate_datasets.name: VertNet
candidate_datasets.role: museum specimen records for colour and locality

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: occurrences that tie colour morphs to habitats

obstacles: Predation trials that measure the survival benefit are scattered across papers rather than one open table.
Background matching can serve thermoregulation or sexual display as well as crypsis.
Photographs over-represent conspicuous and diurnal animals.
assessments.rationale: Colour match and predator survival form a clear confirming and refuting contrast, and published experiments already cover insects and a few birds. Those survival data are not gathered in a single downloadable database, and photo archives only proxy the pattern. A compilation could test a familiar subset of visually hunted prey, with serious but manageable alternative functions of colour.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate genetic correlations between traits expressed at different ages, and compare phylogenetic divergence of larval and adult characters. Independent, stage-specific responses would confirm that selection can modify one age without the other; consistently high cross-age correlations would refute that independence. Age-specific inheritance is proxied by stage-specific expression and quantitative-genetic matrices.

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: stage-specific expression and mutant phenotypes in Drosophila

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: developmental expression and variation for vertebrate model species

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenies on which larval and adult traits can be compared

obstacles: Age-specific genetic-covariance matrices exist for a handful of laboratory species.
Stage-specific gene expression is not the same variable as age-specific inheritance of a selected trait.
Pleiotropy across metamorphosis can hide independent modification.
assessments.rationale: The measurable core is whether characters of different life stages can evolve separately, which quantitative genetics and comparative data can test. Those data are rich for Drosophila and a few other models and thin everywhere else, so the universal and the insect-larva readings are both subset tests. Cross-stage genetic correlation is a real discriminator, but assembling it beyond model organisms would take specialist compilation.

assessments.operationalization: Code mating system, male-combat frequency, and presence of weapons, then fit a phylogenetic regression. The claim would be confirmed if polygynous lineages have higher combat rates and weapon frequencies than monogamous relatives after body size and habitat are controlled; it would be refuted if weapon evolution is independent of mating system. Combat itself is usually proxied by weaponry and sexual size dimorphism.

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: time-calibrated mammal and bird trees for a comparative test

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: mammal body mass, diet, habitat, and life-history covariates

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: current mammal taxonomy against which weapon and mating-system records can be matched

obstacles: Mating system and weapon inventories are spread through handbooks and supplements rather than one global table.
Weapons proxy fighting and can also function in display or predator defence.
Birds are less consistently coded than large mammals.
assessments.rationale: Mating system and weapon presence are standard comparative variables with an obvious phylogenetic contrast, and the trees needed to run it are public. The trait columns themselves still have to be compiled, especially for combat frequency, so the work is months of harmonization rather than a download. Within mammals the test would be informative, with the usual confound that horns and large males are not used only for fighting.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate the genetic covariance between female preference and male song or plumage, and test whether ornament elaboration increases with preference along bird phylogenies. A positive evolutionary response to preference would support the capacity. The wording is a possibility over thousands of generations, so failure in studied species would not refute it, and male-male competition predicts the same ornaments.

candidate_datasets.name: BirdTree
candidate_datasets.role: bird phylogenies for comparing ornament evolution across lineages

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: tail, wing, and body measurements as partial ornament and display proxies

candidate_datasets.name: xeno-canto
candidate_datasets.role: song recordings that document vocal phenotypes, not preferences

obstacles: Female preference time series over many generations do not exist.
Male-male competition and female choice produce overlapping ornament patterns.
Song archives and morphological averages omit the preference-trait covariance.
assessments.rationale: Short-term genetic covariances and phylogenetic associations are available as proxies, and they can show that preference is capable of shifting male traits in particular species. They do not replay the historical, multi-thousand-generation process, and a negative result in one clade would leave the possibility claim standing. Existing public data therefore test a restricted, present-day proxy and do not separate female choice from other sexual selection.

assessments.operationalization: Restrict the comparison to species whose sexes share diet and foraging stratum, then partition sexual dimorphism into ornamental versus ecological traits and ask which class accounts for more of the sex difference. Ornament-dominated dimorphism would support a mainly sexual-selection reading; ecological dimorphism in those same species would count against it. Causation remains an inference from the partition.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits
candidate_datasets.role: species-level diet and foraging stratum as the shared niche background, without a sex split

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: morphological measurements for birds, mostly unsexed

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenies for separating shared ancestry from sex-specific divergence

obstacles: Most global trait tables are not sex-specific, so ornament dimorphism must be joined from scattered sources.
Calling a trait an ornament already leans on the sexual-selection hypothesis.
Niche similarity between sexes is coarsely coded.
assessments.rationale: Shared habits and structural sex differences can be scored with existing ecological and morphological compilations, but only after a substantial join to sex-specific descriptions. The historical claim that sexual selection was the main cause is harder: the same dimorphism is predicted by niche divergence, predation, and drift. The feasible analysis is a comparative partition for birds and mammals, not a direct reconstruction of cause.

assessments.operationalization: Match floral measurements to the morphology of recorded insect visitors and test whether changes on the two phylogenies are correlated. Trait matching beyond a null of random visits would support mutual modification; matching explained entirely by pollinators filtering flowers that already fit would refute reciprocal adaptation. Simultaneous versus sequential change is a further, weaker contrast using relative timing on time-calibrated trees.

candidate_datasets.name: GloBI
candidate_datasets.role: records of flower-insect visitation and pollination

candidate_datasets.name: Web of Life
candidate_datasets.role: ecological networks of plants and pollinators

candidate_datasets.name: TRY
candidate_datasets.role: floral traits to pair with visitor morphology

obstacles: Visitor morphology and corolla measurements are only partly in the same databases as interactions.
One-sided adaptation and ecological filtering produce trait matching without reciprocal change.
Network coverage is strong for a few floras and poor for most insect-plant pairs.
assessments.rationale: Trait matching and correlated phylogenetic change are standard tests, and interaction networks plus floral traits make a partial version feasible. Coverage is a subset of flowering plants and their insects, concentrated where networks have been assembled. Matching alone does not show that both parties were modified, or whether the changes were simultaneous, so the analysis discriminates mutual adaptation only modestly from one-sided filtering.

assessments.operationalization: Compile the effect sizes of alleles that have contributed to retained adaptive change, and the frequency of polyploid and other macromutational origins. The strict reading would be confirmed only if preserved adaptations are overwhelmingly built from tiny-effect steps. It would be refuted if large-effect alleles or whole-genome duplications repeatedly constitute the inherited change that is kept.

candidate_datasets.name: GWAS Catalog
candidate_datasets.role: effect sizes of trait-associated variants

candidate_datasets.name: Chromosome Counts Database
candidate_datasets.role: chromosome numbers used to identify polyploid shifts

candidate_datasets.name: Animal QTLdb
candidate_datasets.role: mapped loci of large and small effect on domesticated animal traits

obstacles: Infinitesimally small can be read as a population-genetic limit or as a ban on large mutations, and those readings diverge.
GWAS and QTL samples are biased toward large effects and toward crops, livestock, and humans.
A large-effect allele can still be followed by a long series of small modifiers.
assessments.rationale: Because the wording is exclusive, documented large-effect adaptations and polyploid origins in public genetic and chromosomal databases are directly relevant and do not require a survey of every organism. How small a modification must be before it counts as infinitesimal is contested, which blocks a single decision threshold. The data can challenge the strict exclusion of sudden large change and still leave a gradualist, polygenic reading standing.

assessments.operationalization: Compare vigour and fertility among offspring of crosses between varieties or strains and offspring of close inbred matings, using inbreeding coefficient as the predictor. Higher fitness of the crosses, and lower fitness as inbreeding increases, would confirm the contrast; no relationship, or a reversal after maternal effects are removed, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: sequence data from pedigreed wild and domestic populations used to estimate relatedness

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: variant data for model plants and animals in which inbred and outbred lines are compared

obstacles: Fitness of crosses versus close matings is published experiment by experiment rather than in one open database.
Maternal effects, purging, and heterosis specific to crops can inflate the apparent benefit of crossing.
Wild populations are less completely measured than livestock and cultivated plants.
assessments.rationale: Inbreeding coefficient and fitness components are standard variables, and the confirming pattern is a negative relationship between relatedness of mates and offspring performance. The measurements exist in volume for domesticates and for a smaller set of wild species, but they must be compiled from studies. Once compiled, the contrast is fairly discriminating, with known biological confounds that meta-analysis can partially address.

assessments.operationalization: For hermaphrodites and candidate ancient asexuals, test genomes for meiosis genes, allele divergence, and the age of asexuality. The claim would be confirmed if every well-sampled lineage shows occasional outcrossing or a recent loss of sex. It would be refuted by a lineage that has persisted for many millions of years with no sex and no genomic sign of decline that an occasional cross would be needed to prevent.

candidate_datasets.name: Tree of Sex
candidate_datasets.role: sexual systems, including selfing and asexual lineages

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: genomes of bdelloid rotifers and other putative ancient asexuals

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: placement and age context of asexual clades

obstacles: Rare sex, gene conversion, and horizontal transfer can mimic or mask long-term asexuality.
Many hermaphrodites still lack genomes dense enough for a Meselson-effect test.
Indispensable is a fitness claim that extant genomes record only indirectly.
assessments.rationale: Prolonged selfing or asexuality leaves genomic signatures, and the decisive lineages plus a sexual-system database are public. A universal claim can be challenged by those lineages without sequencing every hermaphrodite, but the flagship cases remain ambiguous because cryptic sex is hard to exclude. The analysis is standard for a small team and still short of a clean confirmation or refutation across plants and animals.

assessments.operationalization: Join sexual system to woody versus non-woody growth form and fit a phylogenetic model, including a regional term for Australia. A higher probability of separate sexes in trees, repeated across orders, would confirm the association; no difference, or a difference confined to one or two clades, would refute it as a general rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Tree of Sex
candidate_datasets.role: plant sexual systems, including dioecy and monoecy

candidate_datasets.name: GIFT
candidate_datasets.role: growth form and regional floras, including Australian checklists

candidate_datasets.name: TRY
candidate_datasets.role: growth form and reproductive traits for a phylogenetic covariate join

obstacles: Growth-form and sexual-system definitions differ among sources and must be harmonized.
Tropical trees are less completely coded than temperate floras.
Separate sexes and woodiness both cluster phylogenetically, so an uncorrected count would mislead.
assessments.rationale: Sexual system and growth form are standard coded variables, and the confirming result is a phylogenetically repeated excess of separate sexes in trees. Global flora and sexual-system databases cover enough orders and regions, including the Australian case Darwin already flagged, for that test. A small team can run the comparative model in weeks; residual gaps would change the estimate, not the design of the test.

assessments.operationalization: Relate the rate of adaptive substitution, or additive genetic variance for fitness, to effective or census population size across species. A positive partial relationship would confirm that larger populations supply more usable variation per unit time; no relationship after mutation rate and life history are controlled would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: polymorphism and divergence used to estimate adaptive substitution and Ne

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: census population sizes and range extent for a subset of species

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: mammal population density and body size as abundance covariates

obstacles: Effective population size is estimated for far fewer species than the claim covers.
Life history and mutation rate covary with abundance and also change substitution rates.
Census sizes on the Red List are coarse and taxonomically biased.
assessments.rationale: Population size and adaptive rate are measurable, and genomic plus abundance datasets support a comparative regression for vertebrates and a few other groups. That is a subset of all species under selection, and Ne is inferred rather than counted. The regression is informative but confounded by life history, so it tests the abundance effect only partially.

assessments.operationalization: Compare speciation rate, geographic range, and richness of descendant clades between lineages inferred to have originated on large landmasses and those from islands or small regions. Faster diversification and wider ranges for large-area clades would support the claim; equal or higher rates for small-area clades, after clade age and sampling effort, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence-derived range sizes for terrestrial species

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: dated phylogenies for estimating diversification of continental and island clades

candidate_datasets.name: GIFT
candidate_datasets.role: island and mainland floras for comparing area and endemic richness

obstacles: Area, island age, isolation, and collecting effort are entangled.
The place of origin of a clade is often ambiguous once it has spread.
Vertebrates and plants are far better covered than terrestrial invertebrates.
assessments.rationale: Range, area, and diversification rate can be assembled from public phylogenies and occurrence or flora databases for major terrestrial groups. Small isolated areas and large continents differ in age and sampling, so a higher continental rate is not a clean reading of faster modification. The analysis can test a restricted biogeographic proxy and would take substantial harmonization of origins and clade ages.

assessments.operationalization: Compare speciation and extinction rates, and the stem ages of living species-poor lineages, among freshwater, marine, and terrestrial clades. Lower origination and extinction in fresh water, plus an excess of old relict lineages, would confirm the claim; equal or higher freshwater rates in well-preserved groups would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: freshwater versus marine habitat for fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: origination and extinction rates by environment

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenies for living-fossil and diversification comparisons

obstacles: Freshwater fossils are preserved less completely than marine shelly faunas.
Relict is a judgment about morphological oddity as well as phylogenetic age.
Habitat shifts move lineages across the categories being compared.
assessments.rationale: Habitat, diversification, and lineage age are available for fishes and for fossil marine groups, which lets a team compare environments. The freshwater fossil record is the weak part of the claim's scope, and poor preservation can manufacture an appearance of slow turnover. Phylogenetic relicts can be counted for living taxa, but that is a proxy for the historical rate claim.

assessments.operationalization: Measure rates of phenotypic and genomic change per generation and per geological interval, and the fraction of co-occurring species showing concurrent directional change. The claim would be confirmed if change is almost always geologically slow, intermittent, and limited to a small minority of species in a region; rapid, simultaneous responses in many co-occurring species would refute the strong reading. The word slowly still needs a declared timescale.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: durations and morphological turnover used to estimate geological rates

candidate_datasets.name: LTEE
candidate_datasets.role: generation-scale fitness gains under continuous selection

candidate_datasets.name: BioTIME
candidate_datasets.role: multi-species abundance series as a proxy for how many species change at once

obstacles: Slowly can mean per-generation selection or the geological appearance of new forms, and those are different tests.
Field estimates of selection differentials are scattered across studies.
Abundance change in monitoring series is not the same variable as selection.
assessments.rationale: Geological rates are estimable from the fossil record, and generation-scale experiments show that selection need not be slow on an ecological clock. Which clock the wording uses is ambiguous, so the same data can be read as compatible or as a counterexample. Selection gradients for whole regional biotas are not in one open dataset, which limits the test to proxies and well-studied cases.

assessments.operationalization: In fossil occurrences, test whether occupancy declines in the intervals before last appearance beyond a sampling model, and in modern assemblages test whether increases in one species are matched by decreases in others. Pre-extinction rarity and negative abundance coupling would confirm the two clauses; extinctions that are as often preceded by high abundance, once sampling bias is removed, would refute the geological clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: occurrences per taxon per time bin before last appearance

candidate_datasets.name: BioTIME
candidate_datasets.role: assemblage time series for coupled abundance change

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: modern occurrence density as a rarity baseline

obstacles: The Signor-Lipps effect makes taxa look rare before their true last occurrence.
Calling the increasing form the favoured one uses the outcome the explanation is meant to predict.
Ecological time series are short relative to extinction.
assessments.rationale: Rarity before extinction is a direct fossil-occurrence question, and public occurrence databases make the analysis a standard weeks-scale project for well-sampled groups. Sampling bias is severe enough that an apparent decline is not decisive, and the ecological zero-sum clause is only weakly tied to those geological counts. The data resolve a biased subset of the pattern rather than the competitive mechanism across fully stocked regions.

assessments.operationalization: When a form expands or a non-native species establishes, compare the decline of closest relatives with the decline of distant co-occurring taxa, in fossils and in modern assemblages. Greater impact on sister lineages would confirm the claim; impact that is independent of relatedness, or stronger on distant natives, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: stratigraphic replacement among related fossil taxa

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: relatedness of expanding forms and the species they overlap

candidate_datasets.name: GloNAF
candidate_datasets.role: naturalized plants used as a modern analogue of new forms entering a flora

obstacles: Co-occurrence and replacement are not direct measures of competition.
Invasions often hit naive distant taxa harder than close relatives, which cuts against a simple test.
Fossil sister-species pairs are rarely resolved.
assessments.rationale: Relatedness and co-occurrence can be combined for plants and for better-known fossil clades, which is a real but partial design. The prediction is close to Darwin's naturalization hypothesis and can be scored with existing floras and trees. Competition is inferred from overlap and decline, and those patterns have other causes, so the test is informative mainly as a comparative proxy.

assessments.operationalization: Regress community biomass or primary production on functional or structural diversity within sites, holding resource supply constant, in experiments and in observational plots. A positive partial relationship would confirm that diversification of structure supports more life; no residual relationship would refute it for the measured communities.

candidate_datasets.name: Cedar Creek Ecosystem Science Reserve
candidate_datasets.role: long-term plant diversity experiments with biomass and productivity

candidate_datasets.name: Nutrient Network
candidate_datasets.role: coordinated grassland plots of diversity, biomass, and nutrients

candidate_datasets.name: TRY
candidate_datasets.role: plant functional traits used to score structural diversification

obstacles: Amount of life can be counted as biomass, abundance, or production, and the datasets emphasize plant biomass.
Environment can raise both diversity and productivity together.
Experimental communities are mostly temperate plants, not the full local biota.
assessments.rationale: Diversity-biomass experiments are public and already designed around this relationship, so the variables and the decision rule are clear for plants. They cover experimental and grassland subsets rather than animals and every kind of local community. Sampling effects and shared environmental drivers keep the causal reading only partly discriminating, and harmonizing traits with plot biomass is a moderate project.

assessments.operationalization: In small plots, compare the mean taxonomic or phylogenetic distance of co-occurring species with draws from the regional species pool. Excess membership in different genera and orders, relative to that null, would confirm the claim; co-occurrence as related as the null, or more related, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: BIEN
candidate_datasets.role: plant plot occurrences and taxonomy for co-occurrence tests

candidate_datasets.name: sPlot
candidate_datasets.role: global vegetation plots at the spatial scale of close coexistence

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogeny for a relatedness null model

obstacles: Without a regional null, any diverse plot belongs to multiple genera by arithmetic.
Habitat filtering can increase relatedness and offset a competition effect.
sPlot access is restricted, and animal assemblages are poorly represented relative to plants.
assessments.rationale: Plot data and phylogenies make a null-model test of coexistence and relatedness straightforward for plants. The claim's small-area scope is well matched by vegetation plots and poorly matched for animals. Rank names are arbitrary and filtering is a serious alternative, so the result would be informative for plants and would still need the null model spelled out in the design.

assessments.operationalization: For each regional flora, compute the naturalized-to-native ratio at genus rank and at species rank, and compare those ratios with a null that draws the same number of introductions from the global donor pool. A greater proportional gain of genera than of species, beyond that null, would confirm the claim; disappearance of the excess under the null, or across most regions, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: GloNAF
candidate_datasets.role: naturalized alien plant species lists for regions worldwide

candidate_datasets.name: GIFT
candidate_datasets.role: native flora checklists at species and genus rank

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: genus membership used in the donor-pool null

obstacles: Genus size and splitting conventions can create an excess of new genera under random introduction.
Some regions have uneven native inventories.
The pattern for plants need not extend to naturalized animals, which are outside the stated scope.
assessments.rationale: The comparison is a pair of ratios with a pre-registered null, and the regional inventories needed to compute it are public and global. Taxonomic rank is a real artefact, but it is handled inside the same analysis by random draws from the donor pool rather than left as an uncontrolled bias. A small team could confirm or refute the floral generalization with standard checklist joins.

assessments.operationalization: Along fossil lineages with phylogenetic trees, score whether morphologically intermediate forms and putative parent species disappear as derived species become established. Concentration of intermediates in older rocks, beyond a preservation null, would support the claim; frequent persistence of intermediates beside their descendants would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: stratigraphic ranges of candidate ancestors and descendants

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: morphological matrices for scoring intermediate character combinations

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: trees linking fossil and living taxa where they have been placed

obstacles: Parent species are rarely identifiable, and naming practices treat intermediates as separate extinct taxa.
Only a few clades have dense fossil and character data together.
Absence of intermediates is also the expected result of an incomplete rock record.
assessments.rationale: The fate of intermediate forms is testable only where fossils, characters, and trees coincide, which is a small and biased slice of lineages. Identifying the parent species is itself theory-laden, so a result can be partly circular. Public databases support case-wise and clade-wise proxies, not a general count of ancestral extinction.

assessments.operationalization: Place fossil species in morphospace and on trees with living members of the same groups, and ask whether fossils occupy positions between living subgroups more often than a random-extinction null. An excess of intermediate placements would confirm the claim; fossils nested inside living subgroups as often as that null would refute a general intermediate-stem pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences and taxonomy matched to living groups

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: published morphological matrices spanning fossil and living taxa

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: backbone trees for living relatives of fossil taxa

obstacles: Character matrices are clade-specific and unevenly published.
Stem-group fossils are expected to look intermediate under the hypothesis being tested, which can shade into circular coding.
Soft-bodied and poorly fossilized groups are almost absent.
assessments.rationale: Morphospace position between living groups is a concrete variable, and many published matrices already combine fossil and living taxa. Those matrices cover vertebrates and shelly invertebrates far better than the full tree of life, so the scope is partial. The analysis is standard but slow to harmonize, and character choice can nudge fossils toward intermediate scores.

assessments.operationalization: Using a rank criterion that does not itself use the measured traits, such as reproductive isolation or node age, compare morphological distances among populations, species, and genera. Steadily increasing distance with time would support the claim; distances that do not scale from variety to species to genus under that independent ranking would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: continuous bird morphology for disparity at population and species scales

candidate_datasets.name: BirdTree
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic depth as an independent axis of divergence

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: genus and species taxonomy joined to divergence

obstacles: Species and genera are often delimited by the size of the morphological gaps under test.
Variety is not a current rank and must be proxied by populations or subspecies.
Cross-taxon measurements of the same traits are rare outside birds and a few model clades.
assessments.rationale: The pattern that named varieties differ less than species, and species less than genera, is close to how ranks are assigned, so a naive comparison has little power. An independent clock or isolation criterion can break that circle for birds, where morphology and trees are both public. That is a proxy on a restricted taxon, and it still does not show that natural selection, rather than any accumulating process, produced the gaps.

assessments.operationalization: Join fossil occurrences in deep time bins to living checklists and phylogenies, and compute the fraction of species, genera, families, and orders with any living descendant lineage. A very small species fraction and a large number of wholly extinct higher taxa would confirm the claim; survival of a large share of ancient species-lineages, or rarity of higher-taxon extinction, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic occurrences and last appearances through geological time

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: living species and higher taxa used to score survival

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: lineage connections between fossil groups and living clades

obstacles: Species-level ancestor-descendant links are almost never resolved, so higher taxa stand in for them.
The fossil record samples a biased subset of past species.
Extinct names can hide surviving lineages that were reclassified.
assessments.rationale: Extinction of orders, families, and genera is directly countable by joining the fossil record to a living checklist, and that half of the statement is within reach of a standard analysis. Whether a particular ancient species has living modified descendants is usually unknowable and is proxied by survival of its higher taxon. The qualitative scarcity of surviving deep-time lineages is robust in well-sampled groups, but it is not a species-by-species resolution of the full tree.

assessments.operationalization: Compare within-population phenotypic variance and germline mutation rate between domesticated populations and wild relatives, and test whether novel conditions raise mutation specifically in the reproductive lineage. Greater domestic variance and a condition-dependent germline mutation increase would support the claim; equal variances after observation effort and population size are controlled, or mutation rates unaffected by conditions, would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY
candidate_datasets.role: trait values for cultivated plants and wild relatives

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: sequences used to estimate mutation rates in domesticates and relatives

obstacles: Domesticates are observed more carefully and kept in larger or more subdivided populations, which inflates apparent variability.
Relaxed selection and new mutations are different causes of the same extra variance.
Paired within-population variances and condition-dependent mutation rates are scattered.
assessments.rationale: A domestic-versus-wild variance contrast is measurable, but the proposed cause, disturbance of the reproductive system by changed conditions, needs a mutation-rate design that existing trait databases do not contain. Public sequences and trait compilations cover some crops and livestock and leave the mechanism entangled with relaxed selection and sampling. The feasible study is a partial proxy, not a direct test of induced germline disturbance.

assessments.operationalization: Separate direct environmental effects from genetic differences with common-garden or reciprocal-transplant reaction norms, in animals and plants, and compare the size of those plastic effects with the complexity of matched multi-species adaptations. Small animal reaction norms, somewhat larger plant norms, and plastic effects too small to build the coadaptations, would confirm the claim; plastic effects as large as genetic divergence in the same structures would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY
candidate_datasets.role: plant trait values that can be paired with climate, not reaction norms themselves

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: climate gradients along which trait correlations are observed

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: localities linking measured individuals to climate and food environments

obstacles: Common-garden results are scattered in papers and are the actual measurement of direct effect.
Trait-climate correlations mix plasticity, local adaptation, and biogeographic sorting.
Complex coadaptation has no single scalar in these databases.
assessments.rationale: The direct-effect claim needs reaction norms, which exist as many experiments and not as one open database. Climate and trait repositories support only the correlative pattern, which does not isolate the effect of conditions on a given organism. A compiled subset of common gardens could compare animals and plants, with months of harmonization and incomplete taxonomic reach.

assessments.operationalization: Regress hand-wing index, or a flightless classification, on oceanic-island isolation and the absence of mammalian predators, with phylogeny controlled. Concentration of flightlessness on predator-free islands would confirm the geographic pattern. It would not confirm disuse, because selection against the cost of flight predicts the same distribution; a disuse-specific test would require a heritable effect of not flying that is independent of survival differences.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: hand-wing index and range context for essentially all living birds

candidate_datasets.name: BirdTree
candidate_datasets.role: phylogeny for island flightlessness contrasts

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits
candidate_datasets.role: foraging stratum to separate aerial from terrestrial habits

obstacles: Disuse and selection against flight are not separated by wing measurements and island lists.
Predator-free is inferred from island faunas rather than measured predation rates.
AVONET covers living birds and under-represents recently extinct island forms.
assessments.rationale: The association between reduced flight and predator-poor islands is operational and the bird datasets cover that scope well enough for a standard comparative test. The causal wording attributes the condition to disuse, which those datasets do not measure and which selection explains equally well. The resolvable part is the pattern; the mechanism remains confounded.

assessments.operationalization: Compare the proportion of flightless beetles between wind-exposed and sheltered habitats on Madeira and similar islands, and between those islands and mainland relatives. Higher flightlessness in exposed habitats would support selection by wind; equal rates in sheltered habitats and on calm islands would refute that specific agent. A residual role for disuse would remain if wing reduction also tracks lack of use within sheltered sites.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: island and habitat occurrences of ground beetles

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic roster of island beetle faunas to join to wing-state records

obstacles: Wing state is not a field in occurrence databases and must be taken from faunas and specimens.
Madeira is well studied, but a global island-insect sample is patchy.
Disuse and wind selection predict overlapping reductions.
assessments.rationale: The wind-selection hypothesis makes a habitat prediction that can be scored if wing condition is compiled for Madeira and comparable islands. Occurrence databases supply localities, not the morphological variable, so the limiting step is collation. The exposed-versus-sheltered contrast has real discriminating power against a generic island effect and still leaves disuse as a joint cause, which the original wording already allows.

assessments.operationalization: In cave lineages with sequenced eye-loss genes, test for relaxed constraint, positive selection, or pleiotropy with other cave phenotypes. Neutral loss independent of selection would support a disuse-or-drift reading; repeated signatures of selection or pleiotropic benefit would refute the claim that eyes were lost wholly without selection. Mapping disuse onto neutral degeneration is an interpretive step.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: genomes and eye-development genes of cave fishes and other cave taxa

candidate_datasets.name: AmphibiaWeb
candidate_datasets.role: cave and surface salamander distributions and relationships

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: placement of cave species among surface relatives

obstacles: Genetic tests exist for a few models, especially Astyanax, not for most cave animals.
Disuse, as inheritance of an acquired loss, is not a variable in sequence data.
Pleiotropy can look like selection on eyes when selection acted on a linked trait.
assessments.rationale: The claim names a cause, disuse alone, and explicitly sets selection aside, so molecular signatures of selection are relevant in principle. Those signatures are public for a small set of cave species and absent for most of the scope. Where genomes exist, the analysis can challenge the exclusion of selection without measuring disuse directly.

assessments.operationalization: Assemble phylogenies of cave and surface relatives for North American and European clades. Nesting of cave species inside the surface fauna of the same continent would confirm the prediction; clades that unite American and European cave species apart from their local surface relatives would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: sequences of cave fishes, salamanders, beetles, and other regional cave taxa

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: synthesized trees already placing many cave and surface taxa

candidate_datasets.name: AmphibiaWeb
candidate_datasets.role: continental assignments and taxonomy of cave and surface amphibians

obstacles: Some invertebrate cave groups are still sparsely sequenced.
Introductions and long-distance subterranean dispersal can create transcontinental relatives.
Published trees differ in markers and species sampling and need a common rooting.
assessments.rationale: The prediction is a tree topology with a clear alternative, and sequences plus synthesized trees already cover the American and European faunas named in the scope. A team can assemble clade-by-clade tests with standard phylogenetic methods in weeks to a couple of months. Incomplete sampling would widen confidence intervals; it would not change the contrast between regional nesting and a special cave-to-cave relationship.

assessments.operationalization: Classify range boundaries as coinciding with physiological climate limits or as lying inside those limits where interacting species turn over, then compare the two frequencies. The claim would be confirmed if biotic boundaries are at least as common as climatic ones; it would be refuted if most boundaries match tolerance limits and competitor turnover adds no explanatory power.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: occurrences defining range boundaries and co-occurring species

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: climate at boundaries

candidate_datasets.name: GlobTherm
candidate_datasets.role: physiological limits used to separate climatic from biotic edges

obstacles: Tolerance data exist for a minority of species, so many boundaries cannot be classified.
Species turnover at an edge is a proxy for competition, not a demonstration of it.
Dispersal limitation produces interior edges that look biotic.
assessments.rationale: The relative frequency of climatic and biotic boundaries is a definable ratio, and the same public climate, occurrence, and tolerance sources support it. Coverage of physiological limits restricts the ratio to a subset of taxa, mostly terrestrial ectotherms. Even there, turnover and failed dispersal mimic competition, so the test is informative with a serious confound rather than decisive for the full biota.

assessments.operationalization: Within species, correlate measurements of serial and bilateral homologs and compare those correlations with correlations between non-homologous parts. Stronger covariation among homologs would confirm the claim; correlations indistinguishable from non-homologous pairs would refute it. Genetic correlations in model organisms are a second, mechanistic layer.

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: phenotypic and genetic correlations among segmental homologs in Drosophila

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D specimen media from which paired and serial structures can be measured

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: individual bird measurements of repeated locomotor structures

obstacles: Within-species covariance matrices are published piecemeal, not as a global download.
AVONET does not pair forelimb and hindlimb homologs across animals generally.
Measuring existing scans at comparative scale is months of work.
assessments.rationale: Covariation of homologous parts is a direct statistic with a clear null, so the claim operationalizes cleanly. The measurements are scattered across morphometric studies and model-organism databases, with broad coverage only if new measurements are taken from existing images. Discrimination is good once the data are assembled, and assembly is the limiting step.

assessments.operationalization: For characters given high taxonomic weight, estimate their developmental correlation with other traits and the selection gradient on the character itself. A strong correlation together with a gradient indistinguishable from zero would support the possibility that the character is a useless byproduct; a consistently positive gradient would show that those particular characters are retained by selection, without closing a claim phrased as a possibility.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY
candidate_datasets.role: plant morphological traits, including reproductive structures, with uneven coverage

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: developmental correlations and mutant effects that can show byproduct traits

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: matrices of characters that systematists treat as high value

obstacles: A possibility claim is confirmed by one solid case and is barely refutable.
Failure to find a function is weak evidence that a character is useless.
Selection gradients on fine taxonomic characters are rarely measured.
assessments.rationale: Developmental correlation and a near-zero selection gradient would favour a byproduct reading for a particular character, and fragments of those data exist. The wording only asserts that such characters may arise, so counterexamples do not refute it, and proving uselessness is biased toward the claim. Existing datasets support case studies, not a general decision.

assessments.operationalization: On phylogenies, score reduction of structures that have lost their function and ask whether a neighbouring structure enlarges in compensation. Reduction without obligatory enlargement would support the economy clause; enlargement that always requires reduction of an adjoining part would refute that clause. The always-reduced clause would be refuted by functionless structures that are retained without a detectable cost.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: wing and leg measurements for reduced-flight birds

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: gene loss and vestigial developmental pathways in parasites and cave species

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic context for loss and compensation

obstacles: Superfluous is often inferred from the reduction, which circularly supports the claim.
Allometry creates apparent trade-offs that are not nutritional compensation.
Gene loss and morphological compensation are rarely measured in the same species.
assessments.rationale: Compensation versus independent reduction can be compared in birds with reduced wings and in a few genetic models of trait loss. Superfluous is not an independent measurement in those tables, which lowers the force of a positive result. The anti-necessity wording is easier to support, with single well-measured counterexamples to obligatory trade-offs, than the claim that selection always removes every superfluous part.

assessments.operationalization: Compare coefficients of variation in counts of many-times-repeated parts, such as vertebrae or stamens, with counts of parts that occur in small numbers. A decline in variability as the typical count declines would confirm the rule; similar coefficients after equalizing sample size would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: meristic counts, including vertebrae, for a large number of fishes

candidate_datasets.name: TRY
candidate_datasets.role: floral merosity and other plant part counts where recorded

candidate_datasets.name: GIFT
candidate_datasets.role: flora-level trait coverage to extend plant meristic comparisons

obstacles: Within-species count variances are incomplete outside fishes and a subset of flowers.
Low-count parts are often defined as invariant, which can bake in the pattern.
Museum counts and trait databases use inconsistent sample sizes.
assessments.rationale: The rule is a comparison of coefficients of variation and needs little reinterpretation. Fishes and some floral traits are already in public tables, while snakes, many plants, and other repeated organs still require monograph compilation. Within the coded groups the contrast is discriminating if sample size is handled explicitly, and that compilation is the main delay.

assessments.operationalization: Using individual measurements, compare within-species coefficients of variation of traits that are extreme relative to congeners with variation in ordinary traits, and repeat the comparison for traits that are unusual for a whole clade. Higher variation only in species-level outliers would confirm the rule; no elevation, or equal elevation when the whole group shares the trait, would refute the two clauses.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: individual-level bird measurements from which within-species variances can be computed

candidate_datasets.name: BirdTree
candidate_datasets.role: phylogeny defining allied species and clade-wide traits

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: character matrices for non-bird animals such as cirripedes where published

obstacles: AVONET traits are primarily size and shape, not the secondary sexual characters Darwin emphasized.
Individual measurements are often unsexed and unevenly sampled within species.
Cirripedes and most non-bird animals lack a comparable individual-level table.
assessments.rationale: Outlier status and within-species variance are both computable for birds from a public individual-level morphology table plus a phylogeny. That is a large, clean subset and a weak sample of the rest of animals, and it is thin for the sexual characters named in the scope. Allometry and measurement effort are manageable confounds, so the bird test is informative without covering the full statement.

assessments.operationalization: Within genera, compare within-species variance of traits that differ among species with variance of traits shared across the genus, choosing the traits without using their diagnostic role. Greater variance of the species-level traits would confirm the claim; no difference under that blind choice would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: within- and among-species morphological variances for birds

candidate_datasets.name: BirdTree
candidate_datasets.role: genus membership and phylogeny

candidate_datasets.name: TRY
candidate_datasets.role: plant traits for a parallel comparison inside genera

obstacles: Characters used to distinguish species are often chosen because they vary.
TRY mostly stores species means, so within-species plant variances are sparse.
Generic characters can be conservative by the way genera are diagnosed.
assessments.rationale: The comparison of variances is straightforward in birds, where individual measurements and generic placement are both public. It is partly circular if the traits are the ones systematists already picked as species differences, which is how the historical categories were built. A blind trait set can reduce that bias for birds and still leaves plants and most animals as a compilation project.

assessments.operationalization: Within clades, compare evolutionary disparity in secondary sexual traits with disparity in other measured structures, using sex-specific data. Greater disparity in the sexual traits would confirm the claim; equal or greater disparity in non-sexual traits would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: bird morphology that partially overlaps display structures such as tails

candidate_datasets.name: BirdTree
candidate_datasets.role: phylogeny for within-group disparity

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: trees for extending the comparison beyond birds where sex-specific traits are coded

obstacles: Global morphology tables are mostly unsexed and omit plumage and other ornaments.
Showy characters receive more taxonomic attention, which inflates their apparent disparity.
Sex-specific compilations are dense for a few groups, such as galliforms and lizards, and sparse elsewhere.
assessments.rationale: Disparity of sexual versus non-sexual traits is a standard comparative statistic, and phylogenies for the relevant animals are public. The sexual-trait measurements themselves are still scattered, so existing global tables proxy only some display structures. Attention bias is a real confound and can be reduced by using predefined trait sets, which keeps the test informative for well-coded groups.

assessments.operationalization: For traits that reappear after many generations of absence, test whether the alleles are old segregating variants or recurrent new mutations. Old standing variation would support a tendency transmitted through the intervening generations; de novo mutation recreating the phenotype would support sudden reappearance. Only a few domestic breeds have both the phenotype records and the genomes.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: horse, pigeon, and other domestic genomes in which atavistic traits have been studied

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: annotated variation for domestic species and relatives

obstacles: The transmitted tendency is not directly observed and is inferred from allele age.
Well-genotyped atavisms are a handful of domestic cases.
A phenotype can reappear by either standing variation or new mutation in the same breed.
assessments.rationale: Allele age can separate latent transmission from a sudden reconstitution, which is the empirical contrast in the wording, but only where genomes and pedigrees coincide. Those cases are few and mostly domestic, far from a general law for breeds and wild species. The mapping from a tendency in every generation onto standing variation is reasonable and still interpretive, so the present data support case studies rather than a general resolution.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate the phylogeny of living and recently extinct equids from genomes and reconstruct the striping state of their common ancestor. A single clade whose ancestor is reconstructed as striped would confirm the claim; an unstriped ancestor, or striping confined to nested zebra lineages, would refute the striped-parent clause. Common ancestry itself is a separate and sharper test than the stripe reconstruction.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: genomes of horse, asses, hemionids, zebras, and ancient equid DNA including quagga

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: existing equid relationships to compare with a new genomic tree

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: divergence times for the depth of the common ancestor

obstacles: Striping is evolutionarily labile, so ancestral-state reconstruction can be equivocal.
The phenotype of stem equids is inferred rather than observed.
Partial leg and shoulder stripes in horses and asses can be coded in more than one way.
assessments.rationale: The genus is small, densely sequenced, and includes ancient DNA, so monophyly of the named equids is decidable with public genomes and standard methods. Whether their common ancestor was striped like a zebra is a low-powered reconstruction of a labile trait, and an equivocal result would leave that clause unresolved. The data therefore settle the genealogical part more cleanly than the historical colour pattern.

assessments.operationalization: Compare the axes of within-species variation among congeners, and ask whether a variant of one species phenocopies a trait typical of another, using both morphology and parallel genetic changes. Correlated axes beyond those of distant species would support the claim; uncorrelated variation once shared environments are controlled would refute a general tendency to analogous variation.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: population sequences for parallel variation in sticklebacks, cichlids, and similar models

candidate_datasets.name: GWAS Catalog
candidate_datasets.role: shared genetic associations across related populations

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: genus membership for defining congeners

obstacles: Shared environments can produce parallel variation without a shared inherited constitution.
Analogous variants are documented in case studies rather than a cross-genus database.
Domestic races are better measured than wild congeners.
assessments.rationale: Parallel variation among congeners is measurable in a set of well-sequenced groups, and public sequences plus association catalogs cover those models. There is no general table of analogous varieties across genera, so the scope is partial. Selection in similar conditions and shared genetic constraint both predict the pattern, and they can be separated only where the genes are known.

assessments.operationalization: During intervals when a new form becomes morphologically distinct, test whether parental and transitional populations disappear rather than persist beside it. Early presence and later absence of intermediates, beyond a preservation null, would support the claim; routine coexistence of parent, transitional, and descendant forms would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: temporal overlap of closely related fossil forms

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: character data for recognizing transitional morphologies

candidate_datasets.name: BioTIME
candidate_datasets.role: modern assemblage series as a short-term proxy for replacement

obstacles: Transitional varieties are seldom named as populations in the fossil record.
Incomplete preservation removes intermediates whether or not competition did.
Modern time series rarely span speciation.
assessments.rationale: The process claim requires catching parent and transitional forms in the act of disappearing, which almost no dataset records directly. Fossil ranges and character matrices support a proxy in a few dense clades, and modern abundance series are too short for speciation. Taxonomic practice and missing strata both predict the absence of intermediates, so discrimination is limited.

assessments.operationalization: For sister or representative species, measure the width of the zone where both occur relative to each species' range, and the steepness of abundance decline at the edge. Narrow contact zones and abrupt abundance drops would confirm the claim; overlap widths that are a large fraction of range width, or gradual declines, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: abundance and locality data for measuring avian contact zones

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: occurrences for terrestrial sister species across continents and mountains

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: marine occurrences along depth gradients

obstacles: Abundance, needed for abrupt rarity, is dense for birds and coarse for most other groups.
Depth zonation and deep-sea sister species are sparsely sampled.
Taxonomic splitting can manufacture narrow contacts between newly named species.
assessments.rationale: Contact-zone width and edge steepness are direct geographic measurements, and bird data are already sufficient for a large comparative test. The stated scope also includes mountains and sea depths, where occurrence density and abundance are much weaker, so the full scope is not covered. Sampling and species concepts are real biases, but they do not make the bird-scale result uninformative.

assessments.operationalization: Identify phenotypically intermediate populations between two forms and compare their abundance or occupied area with the forms they connect. Much smaller counts for the intermediates would confirm the claim; intermediates as numerous as the endpoint forms would refute it. Subspecies and hybrid-zone censuses are the operational stand-in for varieties.

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: relative abundance across avian hybrid zones and subspecies

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence density of named subspecies and intermediate populations

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: range maps for the forms being connected

obstacles: Intermediate varieties are under-described, so the rarest ones are missing.
Occurrence density is a poor abundance measure outside well-watched birds.
Hybrid zones can be dense locally even when the intermediate phenotype is geographically narrow.
assessments.rationale: Numerical rarity of intermediate forms can be proxied by abundance and area in hybrid zones, especially in birds. The varieties in the wording are not a stable modern category, and non-bird data are mostly presence-only. Under-description of intermediates biases the test toward finding them rare, which limits how strongly a positive result would count.

assessments.operationalization: Relate the rate of adaptive substitution or phenotypic change to abundance, and test whether more abundant forms replace rarer intermediate ones in time series and fossils. Faster adaptive change in common forms, followed by decline of the intermediates, would support the claim; evolutionary rate independent of abundance would refute the mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: adaptive-divergence estimates to compare with abundance

candidate_datasets.name: BioTIME
candidate_datasets.role: abundance trajectories of co-occurring forms

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: occupancy as a fossil proxy for commonness and replacement

obstacles: Improvement is inferred from later success, which repeats the pattern to be explained.
Abundance and Ne are poorly known for the incipient species in question.
Fossil occupancy confounds true commonness with sampling.
assessments.rationale: The mechanism ties three processes, more variation in common forms, faster improvement, and replacement of rare intermediates, and only proxies exist for each. Genomic rates and abundance series can be joined for a modest set of taxa. Because improvement is hard to score independently of replacement, a positive correlation is only weakly discriminating.

assessments.operationalization: Place bats, colugos, and gliding rodents on a phylogeny and score the locomotor apparatus of the earliest fossil bats. Nesting of bats among gliding mammals, or early fossils built for gliding rather than flapping, would support derivation from a gliding apparatus; non-gliding nearest relatives plus early powered-flight fossils would refute descent from the living gliding groups. An extinct gliding stage with no fossil representative would remain untested.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: relationships among bats, colugos, and gliding rodents

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: mammal genomes underlying the ordinal phylogeny

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: early bat fossils and their stratigraphic context

obstacles: A gliding ancestor could be extinct and unsampled even if living gliders are not close relatives.
The membrane extending to the legs can be an adaptation for flight rather than a leftover of gliding.
Early bat fossils are few, so locomotor inferences rest on a small sample.
assessments.rationale: Ordinal relationships and the earliest bat fossils are public, and a standard tree would show whether bats are derived from any living gliding mammal group. That test is decisive against a pathway through colugos or flying squirrels and does not exhaust an unknown extinct gliding stage. The functional reading of the wing membrane as a trace of gliding remains an inference from limited fossils.

assessments.operationalization: Score species whose diet or foraging habitat conflicts with locomotor morphology, such as webbed feet with terrestrial foraging or climbing morphology with ground foraging. Repeated mismatches would confirm that habit and structure can come apart; a scoring rule under which essentially no species mismatch would refute the existential claim. A static mismatch does not show that habit changed first.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits
candidate_datasets.role: diet and foraging stratum for birds and mammals

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: wing, tail, and tarsus morphology for birds

candidate_datasets.name: BirdTree
candidate_datasets.role: phylogeny to see whether mismatches are scattered or confined to one clade

obstacles: What counts as a mismatch between habit and structure needs an explicit coding rule.
The order of change, habit before structure, is not identified by a present-day mismatch.
EltonTraits records species-level habits, not individual flexibility.
assessments.rationale: Diet, foraging stratum, and locomotor morphology are already tabulated for birds and mammals, so a mismatch census is a feasible comparative analysis. That census can establish that discordant combinations occur, which is the existential pattern. It cannot order the changes in time, because structure lagging habit and habit lagging structure look the same in a static table.

assessments.operationalization: Score optical complexity (pigment, lens, aperture, resolution) across arthropods on an independent phylogeny and ask whether neighboring grades are each optically functional. A continuous series of useful grades would support the possibility of a selective path; a complex eye isolated from any functional intermediate, or intermediates that are optically useless, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D meshes of arthropod and vertebrate heads from which eye-region structure can be measured for a subset of taxa

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: opsin and eye-development gene sequences for comparing photoreceptor homology across grades

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic backbone on which eye grades can be mapped to test whether complexity changes in small steps

obstacles: Living grades are collateral relatives, not the ancestral sequence.
No public dataset scores optical performance across Articulata; those measurements are scattered in papers.
A functional series shows that intermediates are possible, not that selection produced any particular eye.
assessments.rationale: The comparative series Darwin appealed to can be approximated with phylogeny plus morphology, but eye-grade and optical-performance variables are not in one open table, so a team would spend months compiling them. Even a clean series would not reconstruct the historical path or separate selection from shared developmental constraint. Coverage is decent for insects and crustaceans and thin for the vertebrate extension of the scope.

assessments.operationalization: The sentence is a falsification rule: the theory fails if some complex organ could not possibly have been reached by successive slight modifications. No measurement records impossibility of every pathway, and a gap in known intermediates does not decide it.
obstacles: Impossibility of every gradual pathway is modal, not a dataset variable.
Missing intermediates are predicted both by true saltation and by an incomplete record, so the outcomes do not discriminate.
assessments.rationale: The empirical clause that no such organ is known reports a state of argument rather than a measurable frequency. Any organ still lacking a known intermediate is compatible with the rule, because the rule demands a demonstration of impossibility, which comparative and fossil data cannot supply. Scores stay near the floor because there is no decision criterion a dataset could meet.

assessments.operationalization: Code lung versus swim bladder, and flotation versus respiration, on a molecular vertebrate tree and reconstruct the ancestral state for lung-bearing vertebrates. The claim is supported if that ancestor is reconstructed as having a flotation swim bladder and lungs are derived from it; it is refuted if lungs (or a non-flotation air organ) are ancestral and swim bladders arise later inside ray-finned fishes.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: vertebrate phylogeny for ancestral-state reconstruction of air-filled organs

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences of early osteichthyans and sarcopterygians that bracket the relevant nodes

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: published morphological matrices that code respiratory and buoyancy structures in early vertebrates

obstacles: The flotation function and soft anatomy of the deep ancestor are rarely fossilized.
Coding lung and swim bladder as alternative states can smuggle in a homology decision.
Selection as the converting agent is not recorded by character order alone.
assessments.rationale: Public trees and morphological matrices make the direction of the transformation a standard ancestral-state problem, and that direction is the core of the historical claim. Soft-tissue function at the critical nodes is inferred rather than observed, so the flotation premise and the appeal to selection stay out of reach of the same datasets. The analysis is feasible for living osteichthyans and only a proxy for the unknown prototype.

assessments.operationalization: Map electric organs, and the tissues and genes that build them, onto a molecular fish tree.
