candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Sampling-standardized global diversity, origination, and extinction for later Phanerozoic intervals

obstacles: Different standardizations still disagree about whether later diversity is flat or rising.
Later geological periods is an elastic interval, and global species richness is not observed directly.
assessments.rationale: Origination, extinction, and standing diversity are the right variables and are already compiled. The scientific disagreement that remains is largely about sampling and rock volume, which means the same public data do not yet yield one decisive balance test. A restricted marine, genus-level version of the question is analyzable now.

assessments.operationalization: In clades that have both a species-level phylogeny and fossil occurrences, test whether the closest relatives disappear sooner after a species originates than more distant members of the family. Preferential loss of the parent and congeners, beyond shared habitat, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Extinction timing of fossil species that can be placed against their relatives

candidate_datasets.name: NOW fossil mammal database
candidate_datasets.role: Cenozoic mammal occurrences for groups that also have species-level trees

obstacles: Parent and descendant are rarely separable from sister species in the fossil record.
Close relatives share climates and habitats, so they can disappear together without competition between them.
Species-level trees tied to occurrences cover only a few groups.
assessments.rationale: The pattern of which relatives disappear first is measurable only where a phylogeny and a fossil record coincide, a small part of the stated scope. Causation by competition is a further inference that co-extinction under a shared environment also predicts. A small team could run the test for planktonic foraminifera or mammals and would not cover genera in general.

assessments.operationalization: Date marine faunal turnovers with radiometric, paleomagnetic, or chemostratigraphic ages and compare their timing across paleocontinents. Turnover coincident within a geological stage worldwide would support the claim; multi-stage diachrony as the usual pattern would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Marine occurrences with paleocoordinates for cross-regional faunal comparison

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Section ages independent of the fossil lists being correlated

candidate_datasets.name: International Commission on Stratigraphy
candidate_datasets.role: Stage framework and radiometric ages for judging what counts as simultaneous

obstacles: Correlation that uses the fossils themselves makes simultaneity circular.
Independent dates are dense in some periods and sparse in others.
assessments.rationale: Cross-regional marine turnover is densely recorded, and independent age frameworks exist so the test need not use the fossils as their own clock. Agreement within a stage is a concrete criterion matching the broad geological sense of the claim. Coverage is stronger for shelly and microfossil faunas than for every marine group.

assessments.operationalization: For fossil genera binned by age, measure taxonomic or morphological distance to the nearest living relatives and test whether that distance increases with age. No age trend, or ancient forms as similar to living ones as younger fossils are, would refute the general rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Age of fossil genera and whether those genera and families still have living members

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Character matrices for morphological distance to living relatives in covered clades

obstacles: Taxonomic rank is a coarse stand-in for amount of difference.
Living-fossil exceptions are expected under a general rule and have to be scored as exceptions, which softens the test.
Character matrices cover a subset of clades.
assessments.rationale: Age versus membership in extant genera and families is directly tabulated and is the comparison Darwin's taxonomic language supports. A regression of distance on age can be run on occurrence data in weeks, with morphospace as a check in covered clades. Living fossils and rank conventions reduce sharpness without making the age trend untestable.

assessments.operationalization: In character matrices, measure morphological distances among living orders and families with fossils excluded and again with fossils included. Fossils that sit in the gaps and shrink those distances would support the claim; fossils that only repeat living clusters would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Published character matrices that include both fossil and living members of a clade

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic placement of extinct genera relative to living orders and families

obstacles: Matrices cover some clades well and most of life poorly.
The characters that define the gaps are also the characters used to place the fossils.
Harmonizing many matrices into one analysis takes months.
assessments.rationale: Gap-filling is measurable as a reduction in morphological distance once fossils are added, and public matrices exist for many vertebrate and invertebrate clades. They do not cover all organisms, and the placement of fossils is not fully independent of the gaps. The analysis is realistic for several major groups and not for the universal scope.

assessments.operationalization: For pairs of groups with a long later history, compare character distances among their early members with distances among their living members. Early members as distinct as living members, or more so, would refute a backward approach between the groups.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Time-sliced character matrices for distances within and between allied groups

obstacles: Suitable matrices exist for a minority of the group pairs in the scope.
Loss of soft tissues can make older fossils look more alike than the living animals were.
assessments.rationale: The prediction is a directional comparison of distances through time and is well posed wherever a matrix spans both ancient and living members. Those matrices are public but scattered, and a global pair-of-groups test would take substantial harmonization. Taphonomic loss of characters is a real bias toward the predicted pattern, so results have to be restricted to characters preserved in both ages.

assessments.operationalization: Compute faunal similarity between geological stages and test whether similarity falls as the time gap grows, and whether each stage is compositionally intermediate between the stages before and after it. Similarity unrelated to temporal proximity would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Genus occurrences by stage for faunal similarity versus time separation

obstacles: Neighbouring formations can share facies, so environmental tracking imitates temporal relatedness.
Uneven sampling by stage changes measured similarity.
assessments.rationale: Faunal similarity against time separation is a standard calculation on public occurrence data and can be finished in weeks. The intermediacy clause is the same matrix read along the time axis. Facies and sampling are manageable by restricting comparisons to similar environments and by subsampling, and they do not erase a large decay of similarity with time.

assessments.operationalization: The stated test is a competition, under a similar climate, between an extinct fauna or flora and a living one. No existing observation records the winner of that encounter, and modern invasions or trait trends change the contrast into a different question.
obstacles: Extinct species cannot be placed in competition with living ones.
Competitive superiority is not a variable stored in occurrence or trait data without replacing the claim.
assessments.rationale: The statement is a counterfactual about a meeting that the fossil record does not contain. Any real pattern of replacement is compatible with later forms being competitively superior and with later forms merely being different. Proxies require a substantial reinterpretation, so they do not resolve the claim as stated.

assessments.operationalization: For late Cenozoic mammals, birds, and molluscs, compare the relatedness of each region's fossils to that region's living fauna and to the living faunas of other regions. Fossils systematically closest to the local living biota would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: NOW fossil mammal database
candidate_datasets.role: Late Cenozoic land-mammal occurrences by continent for comparison with living faunas

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Regional fossil occurrences of mammals, birds, and molluscs

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Living species distributions used as the successor faunas

obstacles: Later dispersal and extinction can erase an older regional succession.
Similar climates can produce convergent resemblance that has to be separated with phylogenetic affinity.
assessments.rationale: Regional fossil lists and living distributions are both public, and phylogenetic relatedness separates local succession from climatic convergence. Mammals in the later Tertiary are well enough covered for a direct test; birds and molluscs are spottier. The comparison is a standard biogeographic analysis on existing downloads.

assessments.operationalization: Partition compositional dissimilarity among the world's regions into a climate component and a regional component, including matched southern temperate belts. If climate distance accounts for which regions share their biotas, the claim fails.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Species occurrences by region for compositional similarity

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: Climate layers used as the physical-conditions predictor

obstacles: Occurrence data are denser in some countries, which can exaggerate regional differences.
Present climate omits the conditions lineages experienced in the past.
assessments.rationale: Community dissimilarity, climate distance, and region identity are standard variables in two open global sources. Variation partitioning can be run for plants and vertebrates at the regional scale the claim uses. Sampling bias is real and is handled by restricting the test to well-sampled cells and higher taxa.

assessments.operationalization: Measure taxonomic turnover across oceans, mountains, deserts, and large rivers, and test whether turnover rises with barrier age and impermeability after climate is controlled. No residual association between barriers and biotic difference would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Distributions used to measure turnover across barriers

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: Climate covariates so barrier effects are not confused with climate breaks

candidate_datasets.name: EarthByte
candidate_datasets.role: Ages of ocean basins and major tectonic barriers

obstacles: Barriers often sit on climate breaks, so the two predictors are collinear.
Barrier age is well known for ocean basins and poorly known for many rivers and deserts.
assessments.rationale: Distributions, climate, and ocean-basin ages are public and enough to test whether major barriers track biotic differences beyond climate. The age-and-impermeability gradient is cleanest for oceans and mountain systems and weaker for rivers. Collinearity lowers the precision of the split and does not remove the test.

assessments.operationalization: Compare phylogenetic similarity within a continent or sea, across habitats, with similarity between different continents that share a habitat. Habitat matches across continents as close as within-continent relatives would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Species composition within continents, oceans, and habitats

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogeny used to score relatedness rather than shared species names alone

obstacles: Many branches still lack a complete tree, so some comparisons stay at the level of shared genera.
Recent human introductions blur regional affinity if they are left in the lists.
assessments.rationale: Within-region relatedness versus between-region habitat matching is a standard phylogenetic beta-diversity contrast, and both occurrences and a synthetic tree are public. Vertebrates and seed plants are sufficiently covered; many invertebrates are not. Filtering introductions is routine and leaves a decisive comparison for the major regions.

assessments.operationalization: Ask whether regional biotas form phylogenetic clusters on molecular trees built independently of the morphological resemblance naturalists scored, and whether regional trait differences exceed what the physical environment predicts. Shared ancestry can be assessed that way; attributing the differences mainly to natural selection remains weakly separated from other causes.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Synthetic phylogeny for clustering of regional biotas

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Sequences underlying molecular trees that are independent of morphological affinity

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Geographic ranges joined to the trees

obstacles: A tree built from the same traits that display the affinity would make the inheritance test circular.
Selection, drift, and direct effects of the environment are not separated by present distributions.
Joint phylogenetic and geographic coverage is partial for the full living and fossil scope.
assessments.rationale: Molecular relatedness of regional faunas and floras is testable with open trees and sequences, and that test is independent of the morphological pattern it is meant to explain. The further split between natural selection and the direct action of conditions does not fall out of those data. The resolvable part is common ancestry of regional biotas, not the mechanism of their differences.

assessments.operationalization: Compare morphological or genetic divergence of species that entered an isolated region together, as an already competing set, with divergence of species that arrived alone into new biotic relationships. The claim predicts little change in the first case and more change in the second.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Branch lengths of island and continental clades as a proxy for amount of modification

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Co-occurrence of colonists used to approximate which species arrived into the same biota

obstacles: Whether colonists arrived together or alone is rarely recorded in a database.
Time since arrival and population size vary with isolation and can produce the same divergence pattern.
Relevant comparisons are spread across separate phylogeographic studies.
assessments.rationale: The contrast between a co-immigrating assemblage and a singleton colonist is a real comparative prediction, but the arrival mode is not a column in open databases. Trees and ranges support case studies of a few radiations. They do not separate isolation from the other variables that change on islands, so discriminating power stays low.

assessments.operationalization: Compute the share of families and genera confined to one biogeographic region, and test whether genera whose species are phylogenetically closest have smaller ranges than genera whose species are loosely related. Widespread tightly knit genera as the rule would refute the second clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Geographic ranges of genera and families

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic membership used to tally endemism by rank

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Relatedness among species within genera, as a stand-in for most natural

obstacles: Most natural has to be translated into monophyly and short internal branches.
Wide-ranging genera are easier to name and sample, which can bias the range-relatedness correlation.
assessments.rationale: Endemism by taxonomic rank is directly countable from open catalogues and occurrences. Phylogenetic tightness of genera is available for a large share of plants and vertebrates, which is enough to test the correlation with range. Sampling bias toward widespread taxa is a known confound and can be reduced by using well-studied classes only.

assessments.operationalization: For species with range-wide genetic sampling, ask whether gene trees fit one ancestral area followed by spread, or require two or more unrelated origins. A substantial share of species with well-supported multiple origins would challenge the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Georeferenced sequences for phylogeographic origin counts

candidate_datasets.name: BOLD Systems
candidate_datasets.role: Barcode records with locality for single-origin versus multiple-origin tests

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Full geographic ranges against which sampling gaps are judged

obstacles: Range-wide sequences exist for a small fraction of species.
Cryptic species and over-lumped names can look like multiple origins of one species.
Published phylogeographies would have to be compiled, which is months of work at global scope.
assessments.rationale: Single versus multiple origin is a standard phylogeographic hypothesis, and public sequences exist for thousands of species. That is a large subset and far from all species. Where sampling is dense, multiple unrelated origins are distinguishable from spread of one population, so the limit is coverage and compilation time.

assessments.operationalization: Using late Cenozoic plate reconstructions, bathymetry, and sea-level history, test whether now-separate continents, and those continents and oceanic islands, were joined by continuous dry land during the lifetime of extant species. Sustained land connections among them would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: EarthByte
candidate_datasets.role: Late Cenozoic plate and shoreline reconstructions

candidate_datasets.name: GEBCO
candidate_datasets.role: Bathymetry used with sea-level change to test possible land bridges

obstacles: Almost continuously and the period of existing species need explicit time bounds.
Short-lived bridges have to be scored separately from permanent unions.
Classifying an island as oceanic, rather than a continental fragment, is a geological judgment.
assessments.rationale: Bathymetry and plate reconstructions directly record whether dry land connected today's separate continents and oceanic islands in the late Cenozoic. The continuous-union reading is decidable for the major continents and for true oceanic islands. Ambiguity is confined to intermittent bridges and to islands of disputed crustal type.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate the fraction of species in a regional flora whose dried seeds stay buoyant and then germinate after a seawater exposure long enough to cross about 900 miles. A flora-scale fraction far from one tenth, under that protocol, would refute the numerical claim.

candidate_datasets.name: LEDA Traitbase
candidate_datasets.role: Seed buoyancy measurements for northwest European species, as a partial experimental sample

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Seed mass and dispersal traits used as a weak proxy for drift potential

obstacles: No public dataset applies one seawater flotation and germination protocol to a whole flora.
Available buoyancy trials often use fresh water and omit germination after drying.
Transit time for 900 miles depends on a current speed the claim leaves implicit.
assessments.rationale: The fraction that survives a stated ocean crossing is a sharp numerical target. Existing trait databases cover buoyancy or seed morphology for some floras and do not contain the seawater-plus-germination trial at flora scale. A compiled subset of published experiments can bound the fraction for particular coasts and cannot confirm the one-tenth figure for a flora in general.

assessments.operationalization: Plot floristic similarity against ocean distance and ask whether similarity remains appreciable over a few hundred miles, including continent-to-nearby-island gaps, and falls to the level seen between distant continents. Ready floristic exchange between distant continents would count against the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Regional and island plant checklists for similarity versus isolation

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence records used to fill gaps between published floras

obstacles: Ancient land connections and human transport can produce the same distance decay.
Currents, birds, driftwood, and ice are bundled together and are not separate variables in flora data.
assessments.rationale: Floristic similarity against sea distance is computable from open checklists and can show whether distant continents are more distinct than nearby island gaps. That pattern is compatible with occasional short-range transport and also with old geology and trade. The data resolve the biogeographic outcome more readily than which means of transport produced it.

assessments.operationalization: For arctic-alpine species shared among separated mountains and the Arctic, test whether last-glacial fossils occur in the intervening lowlands and whether genetic data show one recent northern population. Deep divergence among summit populations, together with no glacial-age lowland fossils, would count against a glacial-relict origin.

candidate_datasets.name: Neotoma Paleoecology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Last-glacial pollen and plant remains from lowlands between present alpine stations

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Modern arctic and alpine ranges of the candidate species

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Sequences comparing summit and arctic populations of the same species

obstacles: Pollen and many macrofossils are not identified to species.
Range-wide genetic studies cover a subset of the European and North American biota.
Survival on unglaciated peaks and later long-distance dispersal can mimic parts of the relict pattern.
assessments.rationale: Glacial-age lowland fossils and modern ranges are in open databases and can test the geographic half of the relict hypothesis for many plants. Species-level identity of fossils and the genetic unity of summit populations are available only case by case. The full claim is decidable for well-studied European and North American taxa and not for the whole arctic-alpine biota.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate divergence times and ancestral areas for temperate clades shared by North America and Europe, and check Pliocene fossils from Arctic landmasses. Divergences much older than the Pliocene, or no northern fossil connection, would count against this history.

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Published divergence times for shared temperate clades

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Pliocene and Pleistocene fossils from high northern latitudes

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Living temperate ranges in North America and Europe

obstacles: Clock dates for the same clade often span more than the Pliocene.
A Beringian route and a North Atlantic route both fit a circumpolar source.
Very little identity has no sharp similarity threshold.
assessments.rationale: Relatedness of the two temperate biotas, northern fossils, and rough divergence times are all in public compilations. The specific Pliocene timing and a single circumpolar source are softer, because date errors are wide and more than one northern route fits the same trees. The analysis can support or weaken the outline for many clades and not pin down the historical detail.

assessments.operationalization: Compare independently dated temperature proxies and glacial maxima across latitudes through the last glacial cycle. Cold intervals offset by a large part of the cycle would refute worldwide simultaneity; overlap within a few thousand years would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Paleoclimatology
candidate_datasets.role: Ice-core, marine, and terrestrial temperature and glacier records for the last glacial cycle

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Dated paleoclimate series used to compare regions on one timescale

obstacles: Orbital tuning of marine cores builds in some of the synchrony under test.
Tropical and some southern land records are sparser than the polar ice cores.
At least in part simultaneous can be met by a weak overlap.
assessments.rationale: Global proxy compilations already align last-glacial temperature and ice extent on shared age models. A small team can compare the timing of maxima by latitude with standard age-depth data. Tuning and uneven tropical coverage limit precision, and they leave a clear test of whether the cold interval was broadly shared.

assessments.operationalization: Compare species identity and phylogenetic relatedness among temperate lowland floras and high-mountain floras, including tropical mountains, with relatedness of those floras to tropical lowlands. Mountain and temperate floras that are generally unrelated would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Alpine and lowland plant checklists for shared and related species

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence records of temperate and mountain plants worldwide

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic distance among species that are not identical

obstacles: Tropical alpine inventories and DNA coverage are thinner than European mountain floras.
Closely related needs a fixed rank or a phylogenetic-distance cutoff.
assessments.rationale: Checklist and occurrence data can count shared species and shared genera between mountain and temperate floras worldwide. Phylogenetic distance covers the distinct-but-allied clause for a large fraction of seed plants. Tropical mountains are the weak geographic slice, and the temperate and northern-alpine comparison is already well populated.

assessments.operationalization: For plant clades disjunct between the hemispheres, infer dispersal direction from ancestral-area reconstruction and test whether north-to-south events predominate. Counts of direction do not by themselves show that natural selection on a larger northern land area caused the asymmetry.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Hemispheric ranges of disjunct plant clades

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Trees used for ancestral-area direction of dispersal

obstacles: Ancestral-area results move when extinction or northern sampling bias is modeled differently.
Direction of spread does not measure dominating power or demonstrate selection.
Amphitropical clades have been studied one at a time and are not one analysis-ready table.
assessments.rationale: A predominance of north-to-south events is inferable for clades that already have trees and range data, which is a subset of southern disjunct plants. The selective-dominance explanation is an extra causal claim those reconstructions do not decide. Compilation and sensitivity to sampling keep the directional test partial.

assessments.operationalization: Count naturalized European species established in the Río de la Plata region and in Australia, and naturalized southern-hemisphere species established in Europe. A symmetric exchange, or a surplus of southern species in Europe, would refute the asymmetry.

candidate_datasets.name: GloNAF
candidate_datasets.role: Lists of naturalized alien plant species by recipient region and native origin

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence records flagged as introduced, including animals that plant lists omit

obstacles: Colonial trade and propagule pressure favor European sources regardless of any intrinsic dominance.
Recording has been more intense for European weeds than for southern plants arriving in Europe.
Animal naturalizations are less completely compiled than plants.
assessments.rationale: Naturalized floras with native ranges are tabulated in an open global database, so the Europe-to-south versus south-to-Europe counts are a direct query. Animals can be added from occurrence flags with more cleaning. Propagule pressure explains the asymmetry and does not prevent counting it.

assessments.operationalization: Combine pre-glacial Antarctic fossil plants with phylogenies of southern-hemisphere disjunct genera and ask whether those genera connect through an Antarctic source older than the glacial period. Roots centered only on Australia or South America, with no Antarctic fossil link, would count against the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Antarctic plant fossils from warmer pre-glacial intervals

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Living ranges of southern disjunct genera

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Relationships among the southern members of those genera

obstacles: The Antarctic macrofossil flora is small and geographically narrow.
Continental breakup, later dispersal, and an Antarctic source are hard to separate when divergence dates are uncertain.
assessments.rationale: Antarctic fossils and southern ranges exist in public databases, and trees exist for many of the classic disjunct genera. Together they can test an Antarctic connection for a subset of genera. Date uncertainty and the thin fossil flora leave continental breakup and overseas dispersal as live alternatives for most clades.

assessments.operationalization: Compare geographic range sizes of freshwater species with those of related terrestrial species, and measure how often freshwater genera occur on more than one continent. Ranges no larger than terrestrial relatives, and regionally restricted freshwater allies, would count against the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrences of freshwater plants, insects, molluscs, and other groups

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Freshwater fish ranges as one well-coded class inside the broader claim

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomy and distribution context for freshwater molluscs and other aquatic invertebrates

obstacles: Habitat is poorly coded on many occurrence records, so freshwater sets need extra filtering.
Cryptic species divide ranges that look cosmopolitan under older names.
Enormous needs a comparison group, because there is no absolute range cutoff.
assessments.rationale: Range size and cross-continental genus occupancy are computable for fishes and for several invertebrate and plant groups from open sources. Habitat mislabels and cryptic diversity reduce coverage below the full set of freshwater classes. A comparison with terrestrial relatives in the same clades is still a direct and feasible test of the wide-range pattern.

assessments.operationalization: Intersect native freshwater fish lists among continents, and measure how species are shared among river basins within a continent. One documented native species on two distant continents would refute the never clause; consistent sharing of whole faunas between neighbouring basins would challenge the irregular within-continent pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Native freshwater fish distributions by country, basin, and continent

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Independent occurrence records used to check FishBase range statements

obstacles: Introduced populations have to be removed, and status flags are sometimes wrong.
Distant continents need an explicit list, because neighbouring landmasses exchanged fish across recent land connections.
assessments.rationale: Freshwater fish ranges are among the best-coded biogeographic datasets, and both a global checklist and occurrence records are public. Presence of the same native species on two distant continents is a single-counterexample test. Within-continent basin overlap is the same data aggregated one level down, so both clauses can be scored together.

assessments.operationalization: Relate the genetic connectivity of widespread freshwater plants and small invertebrates to waterbird flyways, and compare documented bird transport of their seeds and eggs with transport by wind or water. Connectivity that follows bird movements more closely than other vectors would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: Waterbird movements and flyways as the proposed dispersal network

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Ranges of freshwater plants and invertebrates to compare with those flyways

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Population-genetic data for connectivity along proposed bird routes

obstacles: Transport experiments and vector comparisons are scattered in papers and are not one database.
People move aquatic organisms widely, which can create the same ranges.
Mainly requires a quantitative ranking of vectors that existing data rarely provide.
assessments.rationale: Bird movements and aquatic ranges are public, and some genetic studies line up with flyways, so a partial association test is possible. The causal ranking of birds over water, wind, and people is not in those databases. The mechanism can be examined for a handful of plants and microcrustaceans and not shown to be the main process worldwide.

assessments.operationalization: Compare native species richness of oceanic islands with continental areas of equal size, with climate included as a covariate. Equal richness once area and climate are matched would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Island and mainland plant species counts on a common area basis

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Vertebrate and other occurrence-based richness for islands and continents

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: Climate covariates so physical conditions are held roughly constant

obstacles: Inventories are far more complete for plants and vertebrates than for insects.
Results depend on excluding continental islands that were once connected to mainlands.
Occurrence density differs sharply among islands.
assessments.rationale: Species-area comparisons with a climate covariate are a standard analysis of open flora checklists and occurrence data. Plants and land vertebrates match the claim's scope well enough for a clear island-versus-continent contrast. Invertebrates remain under-catalogued, which limits the phrase all kinds and does not block the test for the groups with inventories.

assessments.operationalization: For oceanic islands, compute the proportion of species found nowhere else and compare that proportion with mainland regions of similar area. Endemism no higher than on continents, after inventory completeness is taken into account, would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Island flora checklists with endemic status and area

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Global ranges used to check whether island species occur anywhere else

obstacles: Single-island endemics are sensitive to taxonomic splitting and to undersampling of neighbouring islands.
Insects, where endemism may be highest, are the least completely listed.
A raw percentage has to be judged against a species-area baseline.
assessments.rationale: Endemism fractions for island plants are already coded in open flora inventories, and occurrence data can audit whether a species is truly absent elsewhere. Vertebrate islands are similarly tractable. The test is weaker for insects and for tiny islets with incomplete lists, which is a coverage limit inside an otherwise direct comparison.

assessments.operationalization: On the same islands, compare percent endemism among groups ordered by a dispersal measure that is independent of endemism, such as a marine habit or sustained flight. High endemism in the groups that arrive most readily would count against the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Island occurrences of land birds, seabirds, and other groups used to compute endemism

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: Marine mollusc distributions for a low-modification comparison group

obstacles: Inferring ease of arrival from endemism itself would make the test circular.
Independent dispersal traits are available for birds and incomplete for shells and insects.
Arrival in a body versus arrival as scattered individuals is seldom recorded.
assessments.rationale: Endemism by group on the same islands is computable from checklists, and a marine-versus-terrestrial contrast supplies a dispersal axis that is not defined by the endemism figures. The in-a-body clause and the finer ranking of arrival ability are not in those data. The test works for a few dispersal classes and stays confounded for the rest.

assessments.operationalization: Compare growth form of island endemics with their closest mainland relatives and ask whether shifts from herb to shrub or tree are concentrated on oceanic islands that lacked tree colonists in that clade. Woodiness that arrived already evolved on the mainland would fail the in-situ selection scenario.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Woodiness and growth form of island and mainland species

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Island floras linked to growth-form traits

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Sister-group relationships used to tell in-situ change from arrival of already woody plants

obstacles: Ancestral growth form and sister-species pairs are not stored as one global analysis table.
Woody colonists establishing more easily than herbs imitates evolution of woodiness after arrival.
The selection mechanism is stronger than the woodiness pattern alone.
assessments.rationale: Island woodiness relative to mainland relatives is recoverable from trait databases and floras for many clades. Separating colonization by woody lineages from change after arrival needs a tree and is only partly assembled. The adaptive story about stature under selection is an interpretation of that pattern, so the data resolve the comparative prediction more than the mechanism.

assessments.operationalization: List oceanic islands, set aside continental fragments and recorded introductions, and test whether any native frog, toad, or newt is present. A native amphibian on a clearly oceanic island would refute universal natural absence.

candidate_datasets.name: AmphibiaWeb
candidate_datasets.role: Native amphibian distributions, including island occurrences and introductions

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Independent occurrence records for island amphibians

obstacles: Some Pacific islands sit on arcs or fragments whose oceanic status is disputed.
Introduced frogs are now widespread and have to be separated from native status.
assessments.rationale: Native amphibian presence on islands is a presence-absence question with two open distribution sources. Geological classification of islands is available from the same plate and bathymetric data used elsewhere and is the main judgment call. A single confirmed native population on a never-connected oceanic island decides the universal wording.

assessments.operationalization: Measure each island's minimum distance to a continent or large continental island and record whether it has a native non-flying terrestrial mammal. A confirmed native land mammal beyond about 300 miles would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Native non-volant mammal lists by island

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence records used to check island mammal status

candidate_datasets.name: GEBCO
candidate_datasets.role: Bathymetry and shoreline geography for distance to the nearest continent

obstacles: The result depends on what counts as a great continental island and on using over-water distance.
A few island mammals have disputed native status or may have arrived with people.
assessments.rationale: Island mammal lists and shoreline geography are public, and the 300-mile threshold is an explicit cutoff. Excluding bats and domestic animals matches the claim's own scope. Disputed native status affects a handful of cases and can be treated as a sensitivity check around an otherwise direct test.

assessments.operationalization: Score bat presence, and the fraction of bat species endemic to the island, across oceanic islands ordered by isolation. Absence of bats from most remote islands, or no rise in endemism with isolation, would count against the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Island bat lists and endemic species

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Bat occurrences used to audit presence on islands missing from checklists

obstacles: Small islands are poorly surveyed for bats, so absence is weaker evidence than presence.
Almost every island needs a minimum size, because tiny islets are poor bat habitat.
Endemism depends on whether island populations are ranked as species.
assessments.rationale: Bat checklists for islands and archipelagos are public and can be joined to isolation distance. Presence on remote islands and the endemism of those bats are both countable, with a pre-set size cutoff to make almost every operational. Undersurvey of the smallest islets limits absence claims and does not block the test for islands large enough to have been searched.

assessments.operationalization: For continental and near-continental islands, regress terrestrial-mammal species sharing and mean phylogenetic distance to the nearest mainland on minimum intervening sea depth, with geographic distance and island area held constant. The claim is confirmed if greater depth still predicts fewer shared species and more distant allies, and refuted if depth adds no partial association or the slope reverses.

candidate_datasets.name: GEBCO
candidate_datasets.role: Gridded global bathymetry for the minimum sea depth of channels between islands and the nearest mainland.

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: Range maps of terrestrial mammals used to score species shared between an island and the neighbouring mainland.

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: Species-level mammal phylogeny for measuring how closely allied island and mainland mammals are.

obstacles: Modern depth is an imperfect stand-in for Pleistocene land connections, because channels shallower than past lowstands were periodically dry.
Introduced mammals and incomplete native inventories can inflate or deflate apparent sharing.
Island area, climate and human history remain confounded with depth even after distance is controlled.
assessments.rationale: Depth, distance, species lists and phylogenetic relatedness are standard variables, and the partial-regression criterion follows the claim's 'independent of distance' wording directly. Open bathymetry, mammal range maps and a dated mammal tree cover most continental islands, with weaker native-status data for small islands. The comparison is a routine spatial analysis, though land-bridge history and introductions keep it from being fully clean.

assessments.operationalization: For oceanic-island endemics, compare phylogenetic distance to relatives on the nearest continent or nearby islands with distance to biotas in climatically more similar but geographically farther regions. The claim is confirmed if nearest-source relatives are closer in a large majority of well-sampled clades, and refuted if climate-matching distant regions win about as often.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence records used to assign endemic island taxa and candidate source regions.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Synthetic phylogeny for placing island endemics relative to continental relatives.

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: Climate layers for identifying distant regions whose physical conditions resemble an island more than the nearest mainland does.

obstacles: Most invertebrate and many plant endemics are still missing from phylogenetic trees, so the testable set is biased toward vertebrates and well-studied floras.
Extinct source populations on the nearest continent can make a living relative look farther away than the historical source.
Ocean currents and wind can make the biologically accessible source differ from the nearest shoreline.
assessments.rationale: Nearest-continent versus climate-matched distant region is a direct decision rule, and public occurrences, climate layers and a synthetic tree supply the variables for well-studied archipelagos. Coverage falls well short of every endemic plant and animal, so the 'almost universal' scope is only partly in reach. Where trees and inventories exist, multiple colonizations and missing mainland sisters are manageable biases rather than fatal ones.

assessments.operationalization: Within each oceanic archipelago, test whether endemic species on different islands are reciprocally closer, or form a single clade, relative to species from every other region. The claim is confirmed if within-archipelago phylogenetic distances are consistently the shortest, and refuted if closest relatives usually lie outside the archipelago.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic placement of island endemics to compare within-archipelago and external relatives.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Public sequences for rebuilding clade trees where the synthetic tree is poorly resolved.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Locality records used to assign endemics to islands within an archipelago.

obstacles: Unsampled continental relatives can make an archipelago radiation look monophyletic when it is not.
Many endemic invertebrates and plants have no sequences, so existing trees over-represent famous radiations.
Repeated colonizations of the same archipelago are a real biological alternative and require dense geographic sampling to detect.
assessments.rationale: Monophyly, or shorter within-archipelago distances, is a standard phylogenetic criterion and matches the claim without much reinterpretation. Sequence archives and occurrence data support that test for many vertebrates and some plants, and leave most of the world's island endemics unplaced. The analysis itself is ordinary; assembling a taxonomically balanced sample is what pushes the work beyond a quick study.

assessments.operationalization: For regional floras and faunas, compare the phylogenetic distance of naturalised species to the native biota, and the fraction whose genus is absent from the natives, against a null draw from the pool of species that could have been introduced. The claim is confirmed if successful naturalisations are concentrated in genera missing from the region, and refuted if they are as closely allied to natives as the introduction pool.

candidate_datasets.name: GloNAF
candidate_datasets.role: Global lists of naturalised alien plant species by region, for comparison with native floras.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic distances between naturalised species and the native species of the recipient region.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Introduced-status occurrences that extend the same comparison from plants to animals.

obstacles: Humans preferentially transport particular families, so an apparent excess of distinct genera can be an introduction bias.
The result depends on how the source pool is defined, including which species had the opportunity to be moved.
Animal naturalisation inventories are less complete and less standardised than the plant compilation.
assessments.rationale: Genus absence and phylogenetic distance to natives are measurable readings of 'not closely allied', and global naturalised-plant lists already tabulate the main botanical pattern Darwin cited. Animal coverage is thinner, but introduced-status occurrences are public and the same test applies. The analysis is standard and has been run before; transport bias and source-pool choice are the reasons discriminating power stays moderate.

assessments.operationalization: For islands, sky-islands, lakes and caves, compare the phylogenetic source region of endemics with a dispersal-accessibility model based on distance and barriers, and score whether colonists are phenotypically shifted toward local conditions. The claim is confirmed if the best-supported source matches the most accessible region and derived populations are more environment-matched than their source relatives, and refuted if sources are random with respect to access or phenotypes are unchanged.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenies used to infer source regions of isolated biotas.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrences of island, mountain, lake and cave taxa and of their candidate source biotas.

candidate_datasets.name: Map of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Expert range maps that complement occurrence records for identifying accessible source regions.

obstacles: 'Most readily' requires a dispersal model, and currents, bird vectors and past climates give several competing versions.
Being related to a source shows colonisation, while 'better fitted' needs trait-environment data that most of these biotas lack.
Cave, marsh and lake endemics are inventoried far more unevenly than oceanic islands.
assessments.rationale: The colonisation half can be turned into a source-region test, but accessibility and subsequent adaptation each admit several operationalizations, which lowers the score. Phylogenies and range data cover classic islands much better than caves, marshes and alpine lakes. A broad multi-habitat analysis would take months of harmonization, and adaptation remains a proxy rather than a fitness measurement.

assessments.operationalization: Across pairs of bioregions, count shared species, sister or congeneric pairs, and taxa with unstable species-versus-variety rank, then test whether regions rich in allied pairs also share some identical species and more borderline taxa. The claim is confirmed if that joint pattern is nearly general after controlling for region size and survey effort, and refuted if many region pairs have numerous allied species and no shared species.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Species-by-region occurrence matrices for counting shared and unshared taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: A common taxonomy for scoring identical species, congeners and rank-unstable names.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic proximity used to identify allied or representative species pairs independently of genus names.

obstacles: Taxonomists already split and lump borderline forms most actively where regions share related biotas, so 'doubtful forms' partly reflect effort.
A few very widespread species can create shared-species counts without any special history of migration.
Survey effort and species concepts differ sharply between regions, which can manufacture or hide the predicted association.
assessments.rationale: Shared species, close relatives and nomenclatural borderline cases can be counted from public checklists and trees, so the pattern is operational for vertebrates and seed plants. The universal wording is only as strong as taxonomic practice, which uses the same gaps the claim is about. The analysis is feasible at bioregion scale, with serious circularity around how species and varieties are ranked.

assessments.operationalization: Using an explicit proxy for 'lower', such as non-seed plants versus seed plants or small-bodied versus large-bodied animals, compare geographic range size or number of regions occupied. The claim is confirmed if the lower proxy has systematically larger ranges after correcting for the number of records, and refuted if range size is unrelated to that proxy or runs the other way.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence extents used as a range-size measure across animals and plants.

candidate_datasets.name: GIFT
candidate_datasets.role: Regional floras for comparing how widely bryophytes, pteridophytes and seed plants are distributed.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: A taxonomic backbone for assigning groups to the chosen higher-versus-lower proxy.

obstacles: 'Lower in the scale of nature' has several competing modern proxies, and they do not rank the same organisms together.
Recorded ranges of microbes and minute invertebrates are dominated by where people have sampled, not by where the organisms live.
Better-studied large organisms can look either more or less widespread depending on whether range is measured as a map or as a list of records.
assessments.rationale: The sentence has a measurable biogeographic pattern only after 'lower' is replaced by a grade, body size or propagule size, and those mappings disagree. Checklist and occurrence databases can support a proxy test inside plants or vertebrates and cannot support one across all of life. Sampling bias is large enough that many outcomes would still be compatible with both the claim and its opposite.

assessments.operationalization: Across living and fossil species, test whether phylogenetic distance increases with geographic distance and with separation in time, using divergence dates or stratigraphic midpoints. The claim is confirmed if both partial associations are positive across large clades, and refuted if close relatives are no nearer in space or time than distant relatives once sampling effort is controlled.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic distances among living taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence centroids or ranges for geographic separation among relatives.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences and ages for temporal and geographic separation among extinct forms.

obstacles: Geography has historically influenced which specimens taxonomists treat as separate species, which can tighten the spatial pattern by construction.
Fossil finds are concentrated in well-worked basins, so apparent closeness in time and space partly tracks rock exposure.
Molecular divergence dates are model-based proxies for the temporal nearness Darwin described from fossils and living ranges.
assessments.rationale: Phylogenetic, geographic and temporal distances are ordinary variables, and a positive partial association is an obvious confirming result for a claim qualified by 'generally'. Public trees, occurrences and fossil occurrences cover enough clades to accept or reject that general tendency, even though most fossil species lack a resolved phylogeny. Sampling bias is serious and is the reason discriminating power is not higher.

assessments.operationalization: Ask whether character data from living and fossil organisms fit a branching hierarchy better than non-hierarchical or highly reticulate alternatives, and whether extinction of intermediate branches is required to reproduce the observed gaps between named groups. The claim is confirmed if tree-like structure is strong and simulated divergence without extinction of intermediates fails to produce the observed rank gaps, and refuted if the data are poorly hierarchical or gaps arise without that extinction.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Sequence matrices for measuring how hierarchical living diversity is, against network-like alternatives.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: A global tree summarizing which groups are nested inside which.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil ranges used to ask whether extinct intermediates occupy the gaps between living groups.

obstacles: A pure branching process produces nested groups even when extinction is random, so the specific role of exterminating less divergent forms is hard to isolate.
Building a tree and then reading nested groups off it is circular unless the test is a fit comparison against non-tree models.
Horizontal transfer, hybridization and uneven fossil recovery all reduce the clarity of the hierarchy.
assessments.rationale: Nested taxonomy is visible in existing trees, but the claim is a mechanism, and several branching models produce the same nesting. Sequence archives and the fossil record can test tree-likeness and the presence of extinct intermediates, which is only part of the causal story. A careful model comparison is feasible for major clades and does not cleanly separate this mechanism from simpler alternatives.

assessments.operationalization: Compare traditional classifications with independently estimated molecular trees and ask whether closeness of descent predicts classificatory grouping beyond raw similarity. The claim is confirmed if classifications recover phylogenetic proximity after phenotypic similarity is accounted for, and refuted if they track overall resemblance or ecological similarity instead.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: An independent phylogenetic target for what classifications ought to recover if they track descent.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Current named groups whose nesting can be compared with the tree.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular characters that are largely separate from the morphological resemblance traditional classifications used.

obstacles: What naturalists 'seek' in a natural system is a historical intention, not a column in a dataset.
Gene transfer and convergence also generate similarity, so descent is not the only measurable cause.
Many ranks were revised after molecular trees existed, so congruence with those trees is partly by later construction.
assessments.rationale: Congruence between molecular trees and named groups is a real empirical core, and the needed trees and classifications are public. The wording also makes a conceptual claim about the hidden bond of the Natural System and about descent as the only cause of similarity, which those databases do not settle. The feasible analysis therefore tests a proxy, phylogenetic concordance, rather than the claim in full.

assessments.operationalization: In morphological matrices, partition characters into those tied to special habits and those that are structural, then compare their constancy across large clades and their phylogenetic signal at deep nodes. The claim is confirmed if habit-linked characters are less conserved and less informative for higher groups, and refuted if they are as constant as, or more constant than, structural characters.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Published character matrices in which habit-linked and structural characters can be separated.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Trees on which constancy and deep-node signal of each character class can be measured.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Plant traits linked to habitat and life form, as a functional contrast to conserved floral and anatomical characters.

obstacles: Deciding that a character has been 'little modified by adaptation' is itself an interpretation and will differ among coders.
Systematists already prefer constant characters, so high classificatory value is partly how the matrices were assembled.
Public matrices cover a minority of animal and plant groups, with a strong bias toward vertebrates.
assessments.rationale: Constancy and deep phylogenetic signal are measurable, but the adaptive status of a character is not a standard column and has to be assigned. Existing matrices and trait databases support the comparison in scattered taxa, especially vertebrates and some plant families. Harmonizing those matrices and coding function would take months, and the coding step limits how decisive the result can be.

assessments.operationalization: For genera, families and orders, measure the spread of crown ages, species richness and morphological disparity within each rank, and test whether ranks occupy distinct, non-overlapping bands. The claim is confirmed if within-rank spreads dwarf the differences between adjacent ranks, and refuted if a rank consistently marks a similar age or amount of difference across classes.

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Divergence times for comparing crown ages of taxa that share a Linnaean rank.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Current assignment of clades to genus, family, order and similar ranks.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: A global hierarchy used to place ranked names on a common tree and to count species per clade.

obstacles: 'Almost arbitrary' has no sharp numerical cutoff, so a weak average rise in age from genus to order can be read either way.
Ranks are more nearly commensurate inside one class than they are across animals and plants together.
Some rank changes really do follow the discovery of more allied species, but the historical revision record is less complete than the current ages.
assessments.rationale: Rank, clade age and richness are standard variables, and massive overlap within a rank versus a clean age band is a concrete confirming or refuting pattern. Time-calibrated trees and a global taxonomy already contain those variables for most named higher taxa. The analysis is a short one; the remaining softness is the vague word 'almost', not missing data.

assessments.operationalization: For sister clades, which are equally related to their common ancestor, compare phenotypic disparity or morphological branch length and the Linnaean ranks later assigned to each side. The claim is confirmed if equally close branches often differ several-fold in accumulated modification, and refuted if sister clades are consistently similar in amount of change.

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Sister-clade pairs of equal age against which unequal amounts of change can be judged.

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: Large species-level trees for vertebrates, where unequal rates among sister clades can be estimated.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological matrices for measuring phenotypic modification separately from molecular branch length.

obstacles: The requirement that a natural arrangement must be genealogical is a rule for classification, and datasets do not test the word 'must'.
Molecular branch lengths are abundant, while the amount of bodily modification Darwin meant is available only where morphological matrices exist.
Rank differences between sister clades partly record later taxonomic taste rather than a measured quantity of change.
assessments.rationale: Unequal modification of sister lineages is directly measurable, and public trees make the sister-clade design straightforward for vertebrates. The genealogical 'must' in the same sentence is normative, so existing data test the empirical half. Morphological coverage is the main limit on adequacy, and the rate comparison itself is a standard phylogenetic analysis.

assessments.operationalization: For domestic breeds and wild varieties with known pedigrees or genomic relationships, test whether morphology and named subgroups form a nested hierarchy that matches descent, with deeper splits corresponding to greater modification. The claim is confirmed if breed groups recover the pedigree better than a non-hierarchical clustering, and refuted if varieties of known close descent are morphologically scattered among distant breeds.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Public breed and variety genomes that record pedigree independent of the traits used to name the breeds.

candidate_datasets.name: DAD-IS
candidate_datasets.role: Global inventory of domestic breeds whose named hierarchy can be compared with genetic descent.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic context for wild varieties and the species that contain them.

obstacles: Breeds were often defined by the same external traits used to test nested morphological groups, which makes a purely morphological test circular.
Genomic pedigrees are dense for dogs, horses, chickens and a few crops, and sparse for most domesticated and wild varieties.
Wild 'varieties' are delimited inconsistently, so the natural-variety half of the scope is much weaker than the breed half.
assessments.rationale: Where pedigrees exist, nested breed groups can be compared with descent without adopting a new definition of variety. Public genomes and breed inventories cover a few domesticated species well and leave most wild varieties out, so only a restricted scope is testable. Genomic data break the circularity of testing morphology with groups that morphology defined, at the cost of months of cross-study harmonization.

assessments.operationalization: Code characters shared by many ecologically dissimilar species and ask whether those characters, including rudiments, match an independent molecular tree more often than characters shared by species with similar habits. The claim is confirmed if cross-habit characters are phylogenetically conserved and habit-linked similarities are homoplasious, and refuted if the reverse holds.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Character matrices that record which traits are shared across species with different habits.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular trees used as an independent standard for common inheritance.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Habit and habitat traits for separating ecological similarity from shared structure in plants.

obstacles: Developmental constraint and gene transfer can spread a character across dissimilar species without inheritance from the group's common parent.
Habit categories in matrices are coarse, so 'very different habits' is only approximately known.
Rudimentary structures are mentioned sporadically in anatomical matrices rather than scored across whole classes.
assessments.rationale: The contrast between cross-habit characters and habit-linked resemblances is a usable test of homology versus convergence, once habits are coded. Matrices and molecular trees exist for many vertebrate groups and some plants, not for animals and plants at large. The analysis is standard cladistic fit, slowed by the need to add habit annotations the matrices usually lack.

assessments.operationalization: Measure external morphological similarity, ecological similarity and phylogenetic distance jointly, and test whether distant lineages in similar conditions converge in external form while remaining distant on an independent tree. The claim is confirmed if ecology predicts external resemblance after phylogeny is controlled, and refuted if external resemblance is explained by relatedness alone.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic distance used to show that externally similar species can be genealogically remote.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological characters for separating external, habit-related resemblance from internal structure.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Plant functional traits and habitats for cases such as succulent or aquatic form arising in unrelated families.

obstacles: External form is coded differently in each matrix, so a global resemblance score has to be harmonized.
Some apparent convergence is retained deep homology that a coarse ecological label misclassifies.
Similar climate is only a proxy for the 'similar conditions' that actually shaped the external parts.
assessments.rationale: External similarity, habitat and phylogenetic distance are all measured variables, and molecular trees are independent of the external form being judged. Public trees, morphological matrices and plant trait data cover enough classic and systematic cases to accept or reject the pattern, with plants and invertebrates less evenly coded than vertebrates. The confounding issues are real and are the ordinary ones of comparative methods, not a barrier to a decision.

assessments.operationalization: Through the Phanerozoic, test whether clades that are already species-rich and widespread tend to gain further species while smaller clades decline, and whether that replacement produces the observed concentration of diversity in few higher taxa. The claim is confirmed if prior richness and occupancy predict subsequent expansion and extinction of smaller groups beyond a constant-rate null, and refuted if clade success is independent of prior dominance.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Genus and species occurrences through time for richness, occupancy and replacement among higher taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Living diversity per clade, to score how concentrated species are in a few large groups.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Species totals for living orders and classes whose imbalance the mechanism is meant to explain.

obstacles: Constant-rate speciation and extinction already produce a few dominant clades, so imbalance alone does not show that large groups supplant small ones.
The pull of the recent and better preservation of young rocks make living groups look more dominant than they were.
Linking one group's gain to another group's extinction requires co-occurrence and interaction evidence the fossil record rarely has.
assessments.rationale: Richness, occupancy and extinction through time are in the fossil-occurrence record, so the expansion-and-replacement half can be tested for marine animals. The further claim that this is why all life falls into a few classes is a historical explanation that the same imbalance would suggest under simpler models. A null-model analysis is feasible and would remain ambiguous about the mechanism.

assessments.operationalization: Define phylogenetically isolated groups by long stem branches or high evolutionary distinctiveness, independently of their living species count, then test whether they have unusually few species, unusually large gaps among those species, and richer extinct membership. The claim is confirmed if isolation predicts species poverty and within-group disparity beyond a birth-death null and fossils show former richness, and refuted if isolated groups are not species-poor or show no sign of lost diversity.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Stem lengths and evolutionary distinctiveness used to identify aberrant groups without using their species counts.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Living species counts per genus and family.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Extinct diversity of groups that are species-poor today, as evidence of past loss.

obstacles: Under ordinary speciation and extinction, long-branched groups are often species-poor by chance, so poverty is not by itself evidence of a failed group.
Calling a group aberrant because its species are very distinct, and then treating that distinctness as a result, is circular unless fossils or an independent isolation measure is used.
The fossil record of the relevant stem groups is strong for some vertebrates and poor for most aberrant invertebrates and plants.
assessments.rationale: Isolation, richness and fossil diversity can be measured separately, which avoids defining aberrant groups by the very poverty being tested. Trees and occurrence databases cover living isolation well and past richness unevenly. A birth-death null is essential and is also the reason the pattern, even if found, only partly discriminates relict status from passive rarity.

assessments.operationalization: When a species shares characters with a distant group, map those characters on an independent tree and ask whether they are ancestral for the distant group or shared uniquely with one of its species. The claim is confirmed if such cross-group similarities are usually general plesiomorphies, and refuted if they usually match derived characters of a single species.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Matrices that record the characters underlying supposed cross-group affinities.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Trees on which those characters can be mapped as ancestral or as special to one terminal.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular data for a tree that does not depend on the morphological affinity being tested.

obstacles: Pre-cladistic 'affinity' mixes ancestral resemblance with convergence, so the characters to map are not uniquely defined.
Many matrices were assembled in order to resolve these same affinities, which makes the mapping partly circular.
The living members of a group are an incomplete sample of the ancient parent group whose characters the claim invokes.
assessments.rationale: Character mapping can separate a general resemblance to a group from a special resemblance to one species, which is the empirical contrast in the sentence. The required matrices exist for scattered taxa rather than for every cross-group affinity Darwin had in mind. Months of character coding would still leave a moderate risk that the result restates how the characters were chosen.

assessments.operationalization: For vertebrate classes and other well-fossilized higher groups, test whether stem fossils occupy morphological positions between the living classes and whether denser sampling shrinks the gaps. The claim is confirmed if connecting series are present and stratigraphically early, as with the dinosaur-bird transition, and refuted if a densely sampled class boundary shows a persistent morphological break with no intermediate stem forms.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrences and ages of stem fossils that would fill gaps between higher groups.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological matrices placing fossil and living taxa in a common character space.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic framework for distinguishing stem connectors from members of the living crown groups.

obstacles: Soft-bodied and microscopic groups rarely preserve the intermediate anatomies the claim requires, so the test is strongest for skeletonized vertebrates.
A fossil can narrow a gap without showing that the missing forms were utterly destroyed rather than still unfound.
Last appearances are smeared backward by incomplete sampling, which can exaggerate how suddenly a connecting series seems to end.
assessments.rationale: Intermediate stem fossils are a direct confirming observation, and public occurrence data plus morphological matrices already contain the vertebrate series the claim highlights, including birds. A well-sampled class boundary with no intermediates would count against the claim, so the outcome can go either way. Non-vertebrate classes are less adequate, but they do not block a decision for the vertebrate scope Darwin treats as the strong case.

assessments.operationalization: Represent homologous parts as connectivity graphs and test whether, within a class, adjacency order stays fixed while shape and size vary, using gene expression or developmental identity as the homology criterion. The claim is confirmed if transpositions of connection are absent across tetrapod limbs, arthropod limbs and floral organs, and refuted by well-supported reversals of anatomical order.

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: An anatomical ontology that records connections among vertebrate parts.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D specimens from which shape change can be measured separately from connectivity.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative matrices of limb, mouthpart and floral characters across members of a class.

obstacles: Homology has often been defined by conserved connections, so a purely anatomical test can become circular.
Connectivity is coded in an ontology for vertebrate anatomy and is not a downloadable comparative matrix for insect mouthparts, crustacean limbs and flowers together.
Digit identity shifts and homeotic floral changes require an agreed homology standard before they count as transpositions.
assessments.rationale: A no-transposition rule is empirically sharp once parts are homologized independently of their connections. Public anatomy ontologies and specimen repositories cover vertebrate skeletons much better than the full list of organ systems in the claim.
